Dara, A Textbook of Environmental Chemistry and Pollution Control). Seniors say the paper is set from class notes and the shared slides only, so check lists (especially the 'ten commandments') against the slides; importance is an ESTIMATE until past papers are imported
exam_notes: Mini test (10) and mid term (20, one hour) usually cover the first two or three units with definitions, differences and one 'explain with equations/diagram' question; the end term (40, two hours) covers everything, typically a mix of 2-mark definitions, 5-mark 'explain with examples' and 10-mark 'causes, effects and control measures' or 'with a neat diagram' questions. Chemistry-flavoured parts (smog and ozone reactions, BOD/COD/DO/hardness, noise in dB) are where marks separate students; Unit 5 rewards exact lists (EIA steps, LCA phases, the 12 principles) and exact act years.

topics.why: The opening definition of the course: a near-certain 2-mark 'differentiate' or mini-test MCQ, rarely a long question by itself.
topics.gist:
A **natural resource** is anything obtained from the environment that humans use to meet their needs: air, water, soil, forests, minerals, fossil fuels, wildlife, sunlight.

The classification examiners want is by **renewability**:
- **Inexhaustible** resources are not used up by human use: solar radiation, wind, tides, geothermal heat.
- **Renewable (exhaustible)** resources regenerate by natural processes in a human time scale: forests, fresh water, soil, fish, grassland. They stay renewable only while the rate of use is no more than the rate of regeneration (the **sustainable yield**).
- **Non-renewable** resources exist as a fixed stock formed over geological time and cannot be replaced once used: coal, petroleum, natural gas, uranium, metallic and non-metallic minerals. Metals are *recyclable* non-renewables; fossil fuels are *non-recyclable* because burning destroys them.

The key insight: overuse turns a renewable resource into an effectively non-renewable one. Groundwater pumped faster than recharge, forests cut faster than they regrow, and soil eroded faster than it forms (about 2.5 cm of topsoil takes centuries) are all being 'mined'. Other classifications are by origin (**biotic**: forests, animals, fossil fuels; **abiotic**: water, air, minerals) and by development (potential, actual, reserve). Conservation means the 3Rs, efficiency, substitution by renewables, and equitable use, since rich countries consume a disproportionate share. Bharucha's 'role of an individual' (switch off lights, fix leaks, reuse, eat locally, plant trees) is a favourite 5-mark add-on.
key_points: Definition of natural resource with examples.
Three-way classification: inexhaustible, renewable (exhaustible), non-renewable, with two examples each.
Sustainable yield: use rate must not exceed regeneration rate.
Renewable becomes non-renewable when overexploited: groundwater mining, deforestation, overfishing, soil erosion.
Metals are non-renewable but recyclable; fossil fuels are non-renewable and non-recyclable.
Biotic vs abiotic classification.
Conservation strategies and the role of an individual.
formulas: $H \le R$ — sustainable use: harvest rate not more than regeneration rate
$\text{R/P ratio} = \dfrac{\text{proven reserves}}{\text{annual production}}$ — years a non-renewable stock lasts at today's rate
traps: Calling forests or groundwater 'inexhaustible'. They are renewable only conditionally.
Calling nuclear energy renewable. Uranium is a finite mineral, so nuclear power is non-renewable, even though it is low-carbon.
Saying metals are renewable because they can be recycled. Recyclable is not the same as renewable.
Giving examples without saying WHY each belongs in its class (regeneration time scale). That costs marks in a 5-mark answer.
topics.asked_as: 'Define natural resources and classify them with examples' (2-5 marks); 'Differentiate between renewable and non-renewable resources' (2 marks); 'Discuss the role of an individual in conservation of natural resources' (5 marks); MCQs on which resource is non-renewable.

questions.q: Differentiate between renewable and non-renewable resources with two examples of each.
questions.a:
| Renewable | Non-renewable |
|---|---|
| Replenished by natural processes within a human time scale | Fixed stock formed over geological time; not replaced once used |
| Stay available if use rate ≤ regeneration rate | Deplete with every use |
| Mostly low pollution in use | Fossil fuels pollute heavily when burnt |
| Examples: forests, fresh water, solar energy, wind | Examples: coal, petroleum, natural gas, minerals such as iron ore |

questions.q: Why is groundwater in Punjab or Rajasthan sometimes described as being 'mined' like a non-renewable resource?
questions.a: Groundwater is renewable only through recharge by rainfall infiltration. In these regions extraction for irrigation far exceeds annual recharge, so the water table falls every year and deep 'fossil' aquifers that took thousands of years to fill are being emptied. When use rate > regeneration rate, the resource behaves as a finite stock, i.e. effectively non-renewable.

questions.q: Classify natural resources on the basis of renewability with examples, and explain how a renewable resource can become non-renewable.
questions.a:
**Classification**
1. **Inexhaustible**: not depleted by use, e.g. solar radiation, wind, tidal energy.
2. **Renewable (exhaustible)**: regenerate naturally in a human time scale, e.g. forests, water, soil, fish. Remain available only under sustainable use (harvest ≤ regeneration).
3. **Non-renewable**: finite stocks formed over millions of years. (a) Recyclable, e.g. metals like copper and aluminium; (b) non-recyclable, e.g. coal, petroleum, natural gas.

**Renewable to non-renewable**: if the harvest rate exceeds the regeneration rate the stock shrinks every year. Examples: (i) deforestation faster than regrowth leads to permanent loss of forest and soil; (ii) groundwater pumping faster than recharge lowers the water table permanently; (iii) overfishing collapses fish populations below the level at which they can recover; (iv) topsoil eroded in years takes centuries to form. Hence renewability depends on how the resource is managed.

questions.q: A country has proven coal reserves of 150 billion tonnes and produces 1 billion tonnes a year. Estimate how long the reserves last and state one limitation of this estimate.
questions.a:
$\text{R/P} = \dfrac{150 \times 10^9}{1 \times 10^9} = 150$ years.

Limitation: it assumes constant production. Production usually grows with demand, so the reserves will run out sooner; on the other hand new discoveries and better extraction can raise proven reserves.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-renewable resource?
questions.a: Coal formed from plant matter over millions of years and cannot be replaced on a human time scale. Solar and wind are inexhaustible; timber is renewable if harvested sustainably.

questions.q: A renewable resource is used sustainably when:
options: It is used only by the present generation
Its rate of use is less than or equal to its rate of regeneration
It is completely replaced by a non-renewable resource
Its rate of use exceeds its rate of regeneration
questions.a: Sustainable yield means harvesting no faster than the resource regenerates, so the stock does not decline.

questions.q: Discuss the role of an individual in the conservation of natural resources.
questions.a:
- **Water**: fix leaking taps, use buckets instead of showers, harvest rainwater, reuse grey water for gardens.
- **Energy**: switch off lights and fans, use LED bulbs and star-rated appliances, prefer public transport, cycling or car-pooling, use solar water heaters.
- **Soil and land**: compost kitchen waste, avoid overuse of chemical fertilisers, plant trees and grass on bare land.
- **Forests**: use recycled paper, avoid wasting wood products, support afforestation.
- **Food**: avoid wasting food, eat locally grown seasonal food, reduce meat consumption.
- **Materials**: follow Reduce-Reuse-Recycle, avoid single-use plastic, segregate waste at source.
- **Awareness**: spread awareness, take part in campaigns, follow environmental laws.

Many small individual actions multiplied by a large population produce a large saving of resources.

topics.why: Deforestation (causes, effects) and 'dams and their effect on forests and tribal people' are classic 5-10 mark questions; Chipko is a favourite case study.
topics.gist:
Forests cover about 31% of the world's land and about 21.7% of India's geographical area (India State of Forest Report 2021; forest plus tree cover is about 24.6%). The **National Forest Policy 1988** set a target of 33% of land under forest or tree cover (two-thirds in hills).

**Uses.** *Commercial*: timber, fuelwood (still the main cooking fuel for many rural homes), pulp and paper, bamboo, gums, resins, lac, tendu leaves, medicinal plants. *Ecological*: oxygen production and **carbon sink**, regulation of the water cycle (watersheds feed rivers and recharge groundwater), soil conservation, flood control, habitat for most terrestrial biodiversity, local climate regulation, livelihood of tribal people.

**Deforestation**: causes are agricultural expansion, shifting cultivation (*jhum* in the North-East), fuelwood and timber demand, overgrazing, mining, large dams, roads and urbanisation, forest fires. Effects: soil erosion and siltation of reservoirs, floods and landslides, loss of biodiversity and medicinal plants, reduced rainfall and altered climate, more atmospheric CO$_2$, desertification, and loss of tribal livelihoods and culture.

**Dams** submerge large forest areas, fragment habitats and displace tribal people (Sardar Sarovar on the Narmada, Tehri on the Bhagirathi), who often receive poor rehabilitation.

**Case studies**: **Chipko** (1973, Garhwal, Uttarakhand: villagers hugged trees; Sunderlal Bahuguna, Chandi Prasad Bhatt, Gaura Devi at Reni, 1974), **Appiko** (1983, Karnataka), **Silent Valley** (Kerala, saved from a dam, national park 1984), **Narmada Bachao Andolan** (Medha Patkar). Remedies: afforestation, Joint Forest Management (1990), social forestry, protected areas.
key_points: Forest cover of India ~21.7% (ISFR 2021); NFP 1988 target 33%.
Commercial uses vs ecological services of forests (list at least 5 each).
Causes of deforestation: agriculture, shifting cultivation, fuelwood, timber, grazing, mining, dams, urbanisation, fires.
Effects of deforestation on soil, water, climate, biodiversity and people.
Effects of dams on forests (submergence, fragmentation) and on tribal people (displacement, loss of culture, poor rehabilitation).
Chipko (1973, Uttarakhand), Appiko (1983, Karnataka), Silent Valley (Kerala), Narmada Bachao Andolan.
Conservation: afforestation, social and agro-forestry, Joint Forest Management, protected areas, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980.
traps: Confusing Chipko (Uttarakhand, 1973) with Appiko (Karnataka, 1983).
Writing that India has achieved 33% forest cover. 33% is the policy target; actual forest cover is about 21.7%.
Listing only commercial uses. A 5-mark answer needs ecological services too.
For 'effects of dams', writing only about benefits of dams or only about forests and forgetting tribal displacement (or vice versa).
Forest cover vs tree cover: tree cover is patches outside recorded forest; do not mix the two numbers.
topics.asked_as: 'What is deforestation? Discuss its causes and effects' (5-10 marks); 'Discuss the effects of dams on forests and tribal people' (5 marks); 'Write a note on the Chipko movement' (3-5 marks); 'List the uses of forests' (2-5 marks).

questions.q: What is deforestation? Describe its major causes and effects.
questions.a:
**Deforestation** is the permanent removal of forest cover and conversion of the land to non-forest use.

**Causes**
1. Expansion of agriculture to feed a growing population.
2. Shifting cultivation (*jhum*) with short fallow cycles.
3. Demand for fuelwood and timber, pulp and paper.
4. Overgrazing by cattle, preventing regeneration.
5. Mining and quarrying.
6. Large dams and reservoirs submerging forest.
7. Roads, railways, industries and urbanisation.
8. Forest fires (natural and man-made).

**Effects**
1. Soil erosion, loss of fertility and siltation of rivers and reservoirs.
2. Floods and landslides because runoff increases.
3. Lower groundwater recharge and reduced local rainfall.
4. Loss of biodiversity, habitats and medicinal plants; extinction of species.
5. Increased atmospheric CO$_2$ and global warming (loss of carbon sink).
6. Desertification in dry regions.
7. Loss of livelihood, food and culture of tribal and forest-dwelling people.

**Control**: afforestation and reforestation, social forestry, Joint Forest Management, use of alternative fuels (LPG, biogas), strict enforcement of the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980.

questions.q: Discuss the effects of big dams on forests and tribal people.
questions.a:
**On forests**: (i) large areas of forest are submerged by the reservoir; (ii) roads, colonies and canals clear more forest; (iii) habitats are fragmented and wildlife corridors cut; (iv) loss of biodiversity and rare plants; (v) increased pressure on the remaining forest from displaced people; (vi) downstream changes in river flow affect riverine forests.

**On tribal people**: (i) displacement from ancestral land (e.g. Sardar Sarovar on the Narmada, Tehri dam); (ii) loss of livelihood based on forest produce, farming and fishing; (iii) breakdown of community, culture and traditional knowledge; (iv) inadequate compensation and rehabilitation, often on poorer land; (v) health problems such as water-borne diseases and malnutrition in resettlement colonies. This led to the Narmada Bachao Andolan led by Medha Patkar.

questions.q: Write a short note on the Chipko movement.
questions.a: The Chipko movement began in 1973 in the Garhwal Himalaya (now Uttarakhand) when villagers, mostly women, hugged ('chipko' = to cling) trees to stop contractors felling them. Leaders: Chandi Prasad Bhatt and Sunderlal Bahuguna; Gaura Devi led the women of Reni village in 1974. It was a non-violent Gandhian movement. Result: a 15-year ban (1980) on green felling in the Himalayan forests of Uttar Pradesh, and wide awareness that forests protect soil, water and livelihoods. It inspired the Appiko movement (Karnataka, 1983).

questions.q: List four ecological (non-commercial) functions of forests.
questions.a:
1. Carbon sink and oxygen production, regulating climate.
2. Watershed function: regulate stream flow, recharge groundwater, reduce floods.
3. Prevent soil erosion and landslides by binding soil with roots.
4. Habitat for wildlife; conserve biodiversity and gene pools.
(Also: moderate local temperature and rainfall, absorb pollutants and noise.)

questions.q: The Appiko movement for forest protection took place in:
questions.a: Appiko (1983) was the Karnataka counterpart of Chipko, in the Western Ghats (Uttara Kannada), led by Pandurang Hegde. Chipko was in Uttarakhand; Silent Valley in Kerala.

questions.q: According to the National Forest Policy 1988, the target area under forest or tree cover in India is:
questions.a: The NFP 1988 target is one-third (33%) of the geographical area, and two-thirds in hilly regions. Actual forest cover is about 21.7%.

topics.why: Overuse of surface and groundwater, floods and droughts, water conflicts and 'dams: benefits and problems' are standard 5-10 mark questions.
topics.gist:
Of all water on Earth about **97.5% is saline** (oceans); only about **2.5% is fresh**, and of that roughly 69% is locked in ice caps and glaciers and about 30% is groundwater. Less than 1% of all fresh water is easily available in lakes and rivers. India has about 18% of the world's population but only about 4% of its fresh water; per-capita availability (~1,500 m$^3$/year) is below the 1,700 m$^3$ **water-stress** line.

**Uses**: agriculture (about 80% of India's withdrawals), domestic, industry, power generation, navigation.

**Overuse of surface water** dries rivers downstream and destroys wetlands. **Overuse of groundwater** causes: falling water tables, drying wells, land subsidence, sea-water intrusion into coastal aquifers, and more arsenic and fluoride in deep water.

**Floods** (heavy rain made worse by deforestation, encroachment of flood plains and siltation) and **droughts** (failed monsoon made worse by over-pumping, deforestation and water-intensive crops) are both partly man-made.

**Conflicts over water**: Cauvery (Karnataka vs Tamil Nadu), Krishna, Satluj-Yamuna Link canal (Punjab vs Haryana), and internationally the Indus Waters Treaty 1960 (India-Pakistan) and the Teesta (India-Bangladesh).

**Big dams**: benefits are irrigation, hydropower, drinking water, flood control and fisheries. Problems are displacement of people, submergence of forests, siltation, waterlogging and salinity in command areas, water-borne disease, reservoir-induced seismicity and blocked fish migration. **Conservation**: rainwater harvesting, watershed management, drip and sprinkler irrigation, check dams, reuse of treated wastewater.
key_points: Distribution: 97.5% saline, 2.5% fresh; most fresh water is ice and groundwater; <1% readily usable.
Water stress below 1,700 m³/person/year, scarcity below 1,000 (Falkenmark).
Effects of groundwater overuse: falling water table, subsidence, saline intrusion, poorer water quality.
Floods and droughts: natural triggers plus human aggravating factors.
Water conflicts: Cauvery, Krishna, SYL, Indus Waters Treaty 1960.
Dams: list benefits and problems separately.
Conservation: rainwater harvesting, watershed management, micro-irrigation, recycling.
formulas: $\text{Per-capita availability} = \dfrac{\text{annual renewable fresh water}}{\text{population}}$ — Falkenmark indicator (stress < 1700, scarcity < 1000, absolute scarcity < 500 m³/person/yr)
$V = A \times R \times C$ — rainwater harvesting potential (catchment area × annual rainfall × runoff coefficient)
traps: Saying 3% of water is fresh and 'available'. Most fresh water is frozen or underground; less than 1% is easily usable.
Writing only the benefits (or only the problems) of dams when the question asks for both.
Treating floods and droughts as purely natural. The expected answer stresses human causes.
Using rainfall in mm with area in m² without converting mm to m in harvesting numericals.
topics.asked_as: 'Discuss the effects of overutilisation of surface and groundwater' (5 marks); 'Big dams: benefits and problems' (5-10 marks); 'Write a note on water conflicts' (3-5 marks); a small rainwater harvesting numerical (2-3 marks).

questions.q: Discuss the benefits and problems of big dams.
questions.a:
**Benefits**
1. Irrigation for agriculture through canals; more food production.
2. Hydroelectric power, a renewable and low-carbon source.
3. Drinking and industrial water supply to cities.
4. Flood control by storing peak flows.
5. Navigation, fisheries, tourism and recreation.

**Problems**
1. Displacement of people, often tribals, with poor rehabilitation.
2. Submergence of forests, farmland and wildlife habitat; loss of biodiversity.
3. Siltation reduces reservoir life; downstream deltas get less sediment.
4. Waterlogging and salinity in the command area due to over-irrigation and seepage.
5. Water-borne diseases (malaria, schistosomiasis) around reservoirs.
6. Reservoir-induced seismicity (e.g. Koyna, 1967).
7. Blocked fish migration and changed river ecology; methane from decaying submerged vegetation.
8. Risk of catastrophic dam failure; inter-state water disputes.

questions.q: What are the consequences of overexploitation of groundwater?
questions.a:
1. Steady fall of the water table; shallow wells and hand pumps dry up.
2. Higher pumping cost and energy use.
3. Land subsidence as aquifers compact.
4. Sea-water intrusion into coastal aquifers, making water saline.
5. Deeper water has more arsenic, fluoride and iron, causing health problems.
6. Rivers and wetlands fed by groundwater dry up in the dry season.
7. Drought impact becomes more severe.

questions.q: A hostel roof in Bhopal has an area of 500 m². Annual rainfall is about 1100 mm and the runoff coefficient of the roof is 0.8. How much rainwater can be harvested per year?
questions.a:
$V = A \times R \times C = 500\ \mathrm{m^2} \times 1.1\ \mathrm{m} \times 0.8 = 440\ \mathrm{m^3}$

$= 4.4 \times 10^5$ litres per year (1 m³ = 1000 L).

questions.q: Write a short note on conflicts over water with Indian examples.
questions.a: Water conflicts arise when demand exceeds supply and a river crosses political boundaries. **Inter-state**: Cauvery dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu (also Kerala, Puducherry) over sharing during deficit monsoons, settled by tribunal and Supreme Court (2018); Krishna dispute (Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana); Satluj-Yamuna Link canal (Punjab vs Haryana). **International**: Indus Waters Treaty 1960 between India and Pakistan (World Bank brokered); Teesta and Ganga (Farakka) with Bangladesh; Brahmaputra with China. Causes: growing irrigation demand, urbanisation, dams upstream, erratic monsoon. Solutions: tribunals, treaties, basin-level planning and water-efficient agriculture.

questions.q: Approximately what fraction of the Earth's total water is fresh water?
questions.a: About 97.5% is saline ocean water; about 2.5% is fresh, most of it as ice and groundwater.

questions.q: A country is called 'water stressed' (Falkenmark indicator) when renewable fresh water per person per year falls below:
questions.a: Below 1700 m³ is stress, below 1000 m³ scarcity, below 500 m³ absolute scarcity. India is around 1500 m³, i.e. water stressed.

topics.why: Usually one 5-mark question: 'environmental effects of extracting and using mineral resources', sometimes with a case study.
topics.gist:
**Minerals** are naturally occurring inorganic substances with definite chemical composition and structure. They are **metallic** (iron, copper, aluminium (bauxite), zinc, chromium, gold) or **non-metallic** (limestone, gypsum, mica, phosphate rock, sand), plus the **energy minerals** (coal, uranium). They are non-renewable: once mined and dispersed they are gone, though metals can be recycled.

**Uses**: construction, machinery, transport, electrical and electronic goods, fertilisers, defence, jewellery, energy.

Mining passes through exploration, extraction (**open-cast/surface** or **underground**), beneficiation (crushing, washing), and smelting or refining. Each stage harms the environment:
- **Land**: deforestation, destruction of topsoil, overburden dumps, land subsidence over underground mines.
- **Water**: **acid mine drainage** when sulphide ores (pyrite) are exposed to air and water, heavy-metal leaching, silting of streams, lowering of the water table.
- **Air**: dust, smelter SO$_2$ (acid rain), noise and vibration from blasting.
- **Health**: pneumoconiosis (silicosis, asbestosis, coal workers' 'black lung'), accidents.
- **Social**: displacement of tribal people.

**Indian cases**: Jharia coalfield fires (Jharkhand, burning for over a century), illegal mining in the Aravallis (Supreme Court ban), Kudremukh iron-ore mining in the Western Ghats (closed 2005), Bellary iron ore, Sukinda chromite valley (hexavalent chromium in water, Odisha), Panna diamond mines in MP near the tiger reserve.

**Remedies**: eco-friendly mining, backfilling and land reclamation, afforestation of dumps, treatment of mine water, dust suppression, phytoremediation, recycling of metals, and mandatory EIA.
key_points: Definition and classification: metallic, non-metallic, energy minerals with examples.
Stages: exploration, extraction (surface vs underground), beneficiation, smelting.
Effects on land, water (acid mine drainage), air, health and people.
Occupational diseases: silicosis, asbestosis, black lung (pneumoconiosis).
At least one Indian case study (Jharia, Aravalli, Kudremukh, Sukinda).
Control: reclamation, afforestation, mine-water treatment, recycling, EIA.
formulas: $\mathrm{2FeS_2 + 7O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2Fe^{2+} + 4SO_4^{2-} + 4H^+}$ — acid mine drainage from pyrite
$\mathrm{4Fe^{2+} + O_2 + 4H^+ \rightarrow 4Fe^{3+} + 2H_2O}$ — oxidation of ferrous iron
$\mathrm{Fe^{3+} + 3H_2O \rightarrow Fe(OH)_3 \downarrow + 3H^+}$ — orange 'yellow boy' precipitate, more acid
traps: Writing only about mining and forgetting the effects of USING minerals (smelting SO₂, metal toxicity, e-waste).
Calling coal a 'non-mineral'. In the syllabus coal and uranium are energy minerals.
Saying open-cast mining is safer for the environment. It is safer for workers but disturbs far more land.
Not naming a case study when the question says 'with examples'.
topics.asked_as: 'Discuss the environmental effects of extracting and using mineral resources' (5-10 marks); 'What is acid mine drainage?' (2-3 marks); 'Write a case study on mining in India' (5 marks).

questions.q: Describe the environmental effects of extracting and using mineral resources.
questions.a:
**Extraction**
1. **Deforestation and land degradation**: forests cleared, topsoil removed, overburden dumped; land becomes barren.
2. **Subsidence** above underground mines damages buildings and roads.
3. **Water pollution**: acid mine drainage from sulphide ores lowers pH and dissolves heavy metals; tailings silt up streams.
4. **Groundwater depletion** due to dewatering of mines.
5. **Air pollution**: dust from blasting, crushing and transport; mine fires (Jharia) emit CO, SO$_2$.
6. **Noise and vibration** from blasting and heavy machinery.
7. **Health**: silicosis, asbestosis, black lung; accidents.
8. **Social**: displacement of tribal communities, loss of livelihood.

**Use**
1. Smelting releases SO$_2$, causing acid rain, and metal-laden dust.
2. Heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd, Cr) enter food chains and cause chronic poisoning.
3. High energy use in processing increases CO$_2$ emissions.
4. Discarded products create solid and e-waste.

**Control**: land reclamation and afforestation, treatment of mine water, dust suppression, recycling, EIA before new mines.

questions.q: What is acid mine drainage? Write the reaction involved.
questions.a:
Acid mine drainage is acidic, metal-rich water draining from mines and waste dumps where sulphide minerals such as pyrite are exposed to air and water. Bacteria (*Thiobacillus ferrooxidans*) speed the oxidation:

$\mathrm{2FeS_2 + 7O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2Fe^{2+} + 4SO_4^{2-} + 4H^+}$

The water can reach pH 2-3, dissolves heavy metals, kills aquatic life and deposits orange Fe(OH)$_3$ on stream beds.

questions.q: Write a short case study of an Indian mining problem.
questions.a:
**Jharia coalfield, Jharkhand**: underground coal fires have burned since 1916, fed by unscientific mining and abandoned workings. Effects: land subsidence and collapse of houses, emission of CO, SO$_2$ and particulates causing respiratory disease, loss of valuable coking coal, and displacement of thousands of residents. Remedies: fire-fighting by blanketing and filling, controlled excavation, rehabilitation of families under the Jharia Master Plan.

(Alternatives: Aravalli illegal mining banned by the Supreme Court; Kudremukh iron ore in the Western Ghats closed in 2005; Sukinda chromite valley with Cr(VI) contamination.)

questions.q: Name two occupational diseases of miners and their causes.
questions.a:
1. **Silicosis**: inhalation of crystalline silica dust (stone, sand, granite mines).
2. **Asbestosis**: inhalation of asbestos fibres.
(Also: coal workers' pneumoconiosis or 'black lung' from coal dust.) All are forms of pneumoconiosis causing lung fibrosis.

questions.q: Silicosis is a disease commonly found among workers in:
questions.a: Silicosis is caused by inhaling crystalline silica dust from stone crushing, quarrying and sand mining.

questions.q: Acid mine drainage is mainly caused by the oxidation of:
questions.a: Oxidation of pyrite produces sulphuric acid and Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺. Limestone would actually neutralise acid.

topics.why: Bharucha's 'effects of modern agriculture: fertiliser-pesticide problems, waterlogging, salinity' is a reliable 5-mark question.
topics.gist:
Our food comes from crops (rice, wheat and maize supply most calories), livestock and fisheries. **World food problems**: about 700-800 million people are undernourished (FAO) while a large fraction of food is wasted. The causes are poverty, unequal distribution, population growth, land degradation, climate change and conflict. **Undernutrition** is too few calories; **malnutrition** is a lack of specific nutrients (protein, iron, vitamin A, iodine).

The **Green Revolution** (1960s, M.S. Swaminathan in India) combined high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, irrigation, chemical fertilisers and pesticides. It made India self-sufficient in grain but created the problems examiners ask about:
- **Fertilisers**: excess nitrate leaches to groundwater (blue-baby syndrome above 45 mg/L), runoff causes **eutrophication**, soil acidification, loss of micronutrients and soil organisms.
- **Pesticides**: kill non-target organisms (pollinators, birds), **biomagnification** of persistent chemicals like DDT up the food chain, pest **resistance**, residues in food.
- **Waterlogging**: over-irrigation and seepage from canals raise the water table into the root zone, so roots lack oxygen.
- **Salinity**: evaporation from waterlogged soil leaves salts at the surface (Punjab, Haryana, Indira Gandhi Canal area of Rajasthan).
- Monoculture loses crop genetic diversity; **overgrazing** degrades pastures and causes soil erosion and desertification.

**Solutions**: integrated pest management, biofertilisers and organic farming, drip and sprinkler irrigation, crop rotation and mixed cropping, drainage to fight waterlogging, gypsum for sodic soils, and cutting food waste.
key_points: World food problems: hunger, uneven distribution, waste; under- vs malnutrition.
Green Revolution: HYV + irrigation + fertilisers + pesticides; benefits and problems.
Fertiliser problems: nitrate in groundwater, eutrophication, soil acidity, micronutrient loss.
Pesticide problems: non-target kills, biomagnification, resistance, residues.
Waterlogging and salinity: mechanism and remedies.
Overgrazing effects: loss of vegetation, soil compaction, erosion, desertification.
Sustainable agriculture: IPM, organic farming, biofertilisers, micro-irrigation.
formulas: $E_{n+1} \approx 0.1\,E_n$ — Lindeman's 10% law: only ~10% of energy passes to the next trophic level, so plant-based diets feed more people per hectare
traps: Mixing up undernutrition (too few calories) with malnutrition (missing nutrients).
Explaining salinity without waterlogging. The examiner wants the mechanism: high water table, capillary rise, evaporation, salt left behind.
Confusing bioaccumulation (build-up in one organism over time) with biomagnification (increase in concentration up the food chain).
Listing only negatives of the Green Revolution when asked to 'evaluate'. Mention food self-sufficiency first.
topics.asked_as: 'Discuss the effects of modern agriculture on the environment' (5-10 marks); 'Explain waterlogging and salinity' (3-5 marks); 'What is biomagnification?' (2 marks); 'Write a note on world food problems' (5 marks).

questions.q: Discuss the problems caused by modern agriculture with reference to fertilisers, pesticides, waterlogging and salinity.
questions.a:
**Fertilisers**: (i) excess nitrate leaches into groundwater; above 45 mg/L it causes methaemoglobinaemia (blue-baby syndrome) in infants; (ii) N and P runoff causes eutrophication of lakes; (iii) continued use of ammonium fertilisers acidifies soil; (iv) NPK alone leads to micronutrient deficiency and loss of soil organisms and humus.

**Pesticides**: (i) kill non-target organisms such as bees, earthworms, birds; (ii) persistent organochlorines (DDT) undergo biomagnification; (iii) pests develop resistance, so more spraying is needed; (iv) residues in food and water cause cancer, nerve and hormonal disorders.

**Waterlogging**: excessive canal irrigation and poor drainage raise the water table to the root zone; pore spaces fill with water, roots get no oxygen, and yields fall.

**Salinity**: in waterlogged or arid irrigated land, water rises by capillarity and evaporates, leaving Na, Ca and Mg salts at the surface; soil becomes infertile (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan).

**Remedies**: balanced fertiliser use with biofertilisers and compost, integrated pest management, drip/sprinkler irrigation, sub-surface drainage, salt-tolerant crops, gypsum treatment.

questions.q: What is biomagnification? Give an example.
questions.a: Biomagnification is the progressive increase in the concentration of a persistent, non-biodegradable, fat-soluble pollutant at each higher trophic level of a food chain. Example: DDT at ~0.000003 ppm in water rose to ~0.04 ppm in zooplankton, ~2 ppm in fish and ~25 ppm in fish-eating birds, causing thin eggshells and population crashes. Mercury in fish is another example.

questions.q: Write a note on the effects of overgrazing.
questions.a: Overgrazing occurs when livestock numbers exceed the carrying capacity of a pasture. Effects: (i) palatable grasses disappear and unpalatable weeds spread; (ii) trampling compacts soil, reducing infiltration; (iii) loss of vegetation cover exposes soil to wind and water erosion; (iv) organic matter and fertility decline; (v) in dry regions it leads to desertification (e.g. western Rajasthan). Control: rotational grazing, limiting herd size, fodder cultivation, reseeding pastures.

questions.q: Explain, using the 10% law, why a vegetarian diet can feed more people from the same land.
questions.a: Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next. If 1 hectare of grain provides $E$ units of food energy, eating the grain directly gives $E$, but feeding it to animals and eating the meat gives about $0.1E$. So about ten times as many people can be fed when they eat lower on the food chain.

questions.q: Blue-baby syndrome (methaemoglobinaemia) is caused by excess of which substance in drinking water?
questions.a: Nitrate (from fertilisers) is reduced to nitrite in infants' guts, which converts haemoglobin to methaemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen. BIS limit: 45 mg/L as NO₃⁻.

questions.q: Soil salinity in canal-irrigated areas is mainly due to:
options: Rise of water table followed by evaporation leaving salts
questions.a: Over-irrigation raises the water table; water moves up by capillarity and evaporates, depositing dissolved salts at the surface.

topics.why: Renewable vs non-renewable energy with merits and demerits, and short notes on solar, wind, biogas or hydrogen, are common 5-10 mark questions.
topics.gist:
Energy use rises with population and development. India is the third-largest energy consumer, and about 70% of its electricity still comes from coal.

**Non-renewable sources**: coal, petroleum, natural gas (fossil fuels) and nuclear fuel (uranium). They are reliable and energy-dense but finite, and fossil fuels emit CO$_2$, SO$_2$, NO$_x$ and particulates. Nuclear power is low-carbon but has radioactive waste and accident risk.

**Renewable sources**:
- **Solar**: photovoltaic cells convert light directly to electricity; solar thermal collectors heat water or drive turbines. The solar constant is ~1.36 kW/m$^2$ above the atmosphere, ~1 kW/m$^2$ at the ground at noon. Clean, but intermittent and land-hungry.
- **Wind**: power varies as $v^3$, so siting matters (Tamil Nadu, Gujarat). The Betz limit caps extraction at 59.3%.
- **Hydro**: large dams or small hydro; clean, but with ecological and social costs.
- **Tidal, wave and ocean thermal (OTEC)**: site-specific (Gulf of Khambhat, Sundarbans).
- **Geothermal**: heat from the Earth (Puga Valley, Ladakh).
- **Biomass and biogas**: anaerobic digestion of dung or waste gives biogas (55-65% CH$_4$, rest mainly CO$_2$) plus slurry manure.
- **Hydrogen**: burns to water only; produced by electrolysis ('green' when the electricity is renewable). India has a National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023).

India's target is **500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030** and net zero by 2070. **Energy conservation** (efficient appliances, LED lighting, public transport, insulation) is the cheapest 'source'.
key_points: Classification: non-renewable (coal, oil, gas, nuclear) vs renewable (solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, biomass, hydrogen).
Merits and demerits of each source.
Wind power ∝ v³; hydro power ∝ Q × H.
Biogas: anaerobic digestion; composition ~55-65% CH₄, 30-40% CO₂; slurry as manure.
Solar: PV vs solar thermal; intermittency and storage problem.
India's energy mix and 2030 target (500 GW non-fossil).
Energy conservation measures.
formulas: $P = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho A v^3$ — power in the wind ($\rho \approx 1.2\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$); turbine output $= C_p P$ with $C_p \le 0.593$ (Betz)
$P = \eta \rho g Q H$ — hydroelectric power
$\eta_{PV} = \dfrac{P_{out}}{G \times A}$ — solar cell efficiency ($G$ = irradiance, W/m²)
$\mathrm{CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O}$ — combustion of biogas methane
$\mathrm{2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O}$ — hydrogen fuel cell / combustion
traps: Calling nuclear energy renewable.
Writing biogas as mainly CO₂ or as an aerobic process. It is mainly methane, from anaerobic digestion.
Forgetting the cube: doubling wind speed gives 8 times the power, not 2 times.
Calling hydrogen a 'source' of energy. It is an energy carrier; it must be produced using another source.
topics.asked_as: 'Differentiate renewable and non-renewable energy sources with examples' (2-5 marks); 'Write short notes on solar/wind/biogas/hydrogen energy' (5 marks); 'Discuss alternative energy sources' (10 marks); occasional wind or hydro power numerical.

questions.q: Discuss any four alternative (renewable) energy sources with their merits and limitations.
questions.a:
1. **Solar**: PV cells convert sunlight to electricity; solar heaters and cookers. *Merits*: inexhaustible, no emissions in use, suits India's ~300 sunny days. *Limits*: intermittent (night, clouds), needs storage, large land area, high initial cost, panel waste.
2. **Wind**: turbines convert kinetic energy of wind ($P = \tfrac12\rho A v^3$). *Merits*: clean, low running cost. *Limits*: site-specific, intermittent, noise, bird collisions, visual impact.
3. **Hydro**: potential energy of stored water drives turbines. *Merits*: renewable, cheap power, quick to start for peak load, flood control. *Limits*: displacement, submergence of forests, siltation, seismic risk.
4. **Biogas**: anaerobic digestion of cattle dung, kitchen and farm waste gives ~60% CH$_4$. *Merits*: clean cooking fuel, reduces fuelwood use, slurry is good manure, improves sanitation. *Limits*: needs steady feed and warm temperature, low gas output in winter.
(Also acceptable: tidal, geothermal, hydrogen, OTEC.)

questions.q: A wind turbine has a rotor diameter of 40 m and the wind speed is 10 m/s. Taking air density 1.2 kg/m³ and power coefficient 0.4, find the power in the wind and the electrical output.
questions.a:
$A = \pi r^2 = \pi (20)^2 = 1256.6\ \mathrm{m^2}$

$P_{wind} = \tfrac12 \rho A v^3 = 0.5 \times 1.2 \times 1256.6 \times 10^3 = 7.54 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{W} \approx 754\ \mathrm{kW}$

$P_{out} = C_p P_{wind} = 0.4 \times 754 \approx 302\ \mathrm{kW}$

questions.q: A hydro plant has a flow of 10 m³/s through a head of 50 m with overall efficiency 85%. Find the power output.
questions.a: $P = \eta \rho g Q H = 0.85 \times 1000 \times 9.81 \times 10 \times 50 = 4.17 \times 10^6\ \mathrm{W} \approx 4.17\ \mathrm{MW}$

questions.q: What is biogas? Give its composition and two advantages.
questions.a: Biogas is the gas produced by anaerobic digestion of biodegradable matter (cattle dung, kitchen and farm waste) by methanogenic bacteria. Composition: CH$_4$ 55-65%, CO$_2$ 30-40%, traces of H$_2$S, N$_2$, H$_2$. Advantages: (i) clean, smokeless cooking fuel that replaces fuelwood and reduces indoor air pollution; (ii) the digested slurry is a nutrient-rich manure; (iii) improves rural sanitation.

questions.q: If wind speed doubles, the power available in the wind becomes:
questions.a: $P \propto v^3$, so $2^3 = 8$ times.

questions.q: The main combustible component of biogas is:
questions.a: Biogas is about 55-65% methane; the rest is mainly CO₂.

topics.why: Land degradation, soil erosion and desertification usually earn one 5-mark question (causes plus control); man-induced landslides is a common short note.
topics.gist:
Land provides space for food production, forests, grazing, settlements, industry and minerals. Soil forms very slowly, about 2.5 cm in several hundred years, so it is effectively finite. About **30% of India's land is degraded** (ISRO desertification atlas: ~97.8 million hectares, 2018-19).

**Land degradation** is any decline in the land's productive capacity, through soil erosion, waterlogging, salinisation, loss of nutrients and organic matter, chemical pollution, or mining and construction.

**Soil erosion** is removal of topsoil by **water** (sheet, rill and gully erosion, ending in ravines like those of the Chambal in MP) or by **wind** (in arid western Rajasthan). Human causes: deforestation, overgrazing, faulty ploughing on slopes, shifting cultivation, mining, construction.

**Man-induced landslides**: cutting hill slopes for roads, tunnels and buildings, blasting, quarrying, deforestation and reservoir filling destabilise slopes, especially in the Himalaya (Joshimath subsidence 2023) and the Western Ghats (Malin, Maharashtra, 2014).

**Desertification** (UNCCD) is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities. Causes are overgrazing, deforestation, over-cultivation, poor irrigation and salinity, and drought. It is not the same as the advance of existing deserts.

**Conservation**: afforestation and shelter belts, contour ploughing, terracing, strip cropping, check dams and gully plugging, mulching and cover crops, controlled grazing, crop rotation, watershed management and land-use planning.
key_points: Land as a finite resource; soil formation is very slow.
Land degradation: definition and forms (erosion, salinity, waterlogging, pollution, nutrient loss).
Soil erosion: agents (water, wind); types (sheet, rill, gully); human causes.
Man-induced landslides: causes and examples.
Desertification: UNCCD definition, causes, effects.
Soil conservation methods: contour ploughing, terracing, strip cropping, shelter belts, check dams, afforestation.
formulas: $A = R \times K \times L \times S \times C \times P$ — Universal Soil Loss Equation (rainfall erosivity, soil erodibility, slope length, slope steepness, cover, practice factors)
traps: Defining desertification as 'spreading of deserts'. The examiner wants land degradation in drylands due to climate and human activity.
Listing only natural causes of landslides when the topic says 'man-induced'.
Confusing soil erosion (loss of soil) with soil pollution (contamination of soil).
Not naming the types of water erosion (sheet, rill, gully) in a 5-mark answer.
topics.asked_as: 'What is land degradation? Discuss its causes' (5 marks); 'Write a note on soil erosion and its control' (5 marks); 'Explain man-induced landslides' (3-5 marks); 'Define desertification' (2 marks).

questions.q: What is soil erosion? Discuss its causes and the methods of soil conservation.
questions.a:
**Soil erosion** is the detachment and removal of the fertile topsoil by water, wind or other agents faster than it is formed.

**Types**: water erosion (sheet, rill, gully, stream-bank; extreme gullying forms ravines, e.g. Chambal); wind erosion in arid areas.

**Causes**: deforestation; overgrazing; shifting cultivation; ploughing up and down slopes; leaving fields bare; mining and construction; heavy rainfall on exposed soil; strong winds in dry regions.

**Conservation methods**
1. Afforestation and maintaining vegetation cover.
2. Contour ploughing across the slope.
3. Terracing on steep slopes.
4. Strip cropping: alternating erosion-resistant and row crops.
5. Shelter belts / wind breaks of trees in dry regions.
6. Check dams, gully plugging, bunding.
7. Mulching and cover crops.
8. Controlled grazing and crop rotation.

questions.q: Explain man-induced landslides with examples.
questions.a: Landslides are downslope movements of rock and soil. Human activities that trigger them: (i) cutting slopes for roads, railways and buildings removes support; (ii) blasting for tunnels and quarries loosens rock; (iii) deforestation removes the binding of roots; (iv) filling and drawdown of reservoirs saturates slopes; (v) poor drainage and construction loads on unstable slopes; (vi) mining. Examples: Joshimath land subsidence (2023) linked to unplanned construction and tunnelling; Malin landslide, Maharashtra (2014); frequent slides along Himalayan highways. Prevention: slope stabilisation, retaining walls, proper drainage, afforestation, zoning to avoid building on unstable slopes.

questions.q: Define desertification and give its main causes.
questions.a: Desertification (UNCCD) is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from various factors, including climatic variations and human activities. Causes: overgrazing, deforestation and fuelwood collection, over-cultivation, faulty irrigation leading to salinity, mining, and recurrent drought.

questions.q: Approximately what fraction of India's total geographical area is under land degradation or desertification?
questions.a: ISRO's desertification and land-degradation atlas puts it at about 97.8 million hectares, roughly 30% of India's area (2018-19).

questions.q: Ploughing across the slope of a hill to reduce soil erosion is called:
questions.a: Contour ploughing makes furrows along contour lines, which slow runoff and trap soil.

questions.q: Differentiate between sheet erosion and gully erosion.
questions.a: **Sheet erosion**: uniform removal of a thin layer of topsoil over a large area by overland flow; hard to notice. **Gully erosion**: concentrated runoff cuts deep channels (gullies) that cannot be removed by normal ploughing; advanced stage forms ravines. (Rill erosion is the intermediate stage with small channels.)

topics.why: 'Describe the structure of the atmosphere with a neat diagram' is a near-certain 5-mark question; the temperature trend in each layer is the scoring part.
topics.gist:
The atmosphere is the envelope of gases around the Earth: N$_2$ 78.08%, O$_2$ 20.95%, Ar 0.93%, CO$_2$ ~0.04% (~420 ppm), plus water vapour and trace gases. It is divided into layers ('spheres') by the **temperature profile**. (The environment as a whole has four segments: atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere, biosphere. Do not confuse the two.)

| Layer | Height (km) | Temperature | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troposphere | 0-11 (8 at poles, ~18 at equator) | falls 15 → −56 °C (~6.5 °C/km) | ~75% of the mass, all weather, N$_2$, O$_2$, CO$_2$, H$_2$O |
| Stratosphere | 11-50 | rises −56 → −2 °C | **ozone layer** (15-35 km) absorbs UV, which heats it; stable, used by jets |
| Mesosphere | 50-85 | falls −2 → −92 °C | coldest layer; meteors burn; O$_2^+$, NO$^+$ |
| Thermosphere | 85-500 | rises −92 → ~1200 °C | contains the **ionosphere** (O$_2^+$, O$^+$, NO$^+$, e$^-$) that reflects radio waves; aurorae |
| Exosphere | > 500 | very high | thin H, He escaping to space |

Boundaries are the tropopause, stratopause, mesopause and thermopause. The temperature **falls, rises, falls, rises** because of where energy is absorbed: the ground heats the troposphere from below, O$_3$ absorbs UV in the stratosphere, and O$_2$/N$_2$ absorb very short UV and X-rays in the thermosphere.

A **temperature inversion** (warm air over cold air near the ground) traps pollutants, which is why smog episodes happen on calm winter nights and mornings. For the diagram, put altitude on the vertical axis and temperature on the horizontal axis, and draw the zig-zag curve with the layer names and boundaries labelled.
key_points: Composition of dry air: N₂ 78%, O₂ 21%, Ar 0.93%, CO₂ ~0.04%.
Five layers with height ranges, temperature trend, and chief species.
Reason for each temperature trend (ground heating, ozone UV absorption, O₂/N₂ absorption of short UV).
Troposphere holds ~75% of the mass and all weather; lapse rate ~6.5 °C/km.
Ozone layer lies in the stratosphere (15-35 km).
Ionosphere (in the thermosphere) reflects radio waves; ions O₂⁺, NO⁺, O⁺.
Temperature inversion and its role in pollution episodes.
Labelled altitude-temperature diagram.
formulas: $T(z) = T_0 - \Gamma z,\ \Gamma \approx 6.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C/km}$ — environmental lapse rate in the troposphere (dry adiabatic 9.8 °C/km)
$P = P_0\, e^{-z/H},\ H \approx 8\ \mathrm{km}$ — pressure falls exponentially with height
$\mathrm{O_2 + h\nu\ (\lambda < 242\ nm) \rightarrow 2O}$ — photodissociation of oxygen in the upper atmosphere
$\mathrm{NO + h\nu \rightarrow NO^+ + e^-}$,  $\mathrm{O_2 + h\nu \rightarrow O_2^+ + e^-}$ — ionisation in the ionosphere
traps: Putting the ozone layer in the troposphere or mesosphere. It is in the stratosphere.
Saying temperature decreases throughout with height. It alternates: falls, rises, falls, rises.
Calling the thermosphere the coldest layer. The mesosphere (at the mesopause, ~−90 °C) is the coldest.
Drawing the diagram with no axes, no units or no boundary names. The diagram carries marks.
Answering 'spheres' with atmosphere/hydrosphere/lithosphere/biosphere when the question is about the layers of the atmosphere (read the question).
topics.asked_as: 'Describe the structure/layers of the atmosphere with a neat labelled diagram' (5 marks); 'Why does temperature increase in the stratosphere?' (2 marks); 'What is the ionosphere?' (2 marks); MCQs on which layer holds ozone or weather.

questions.q: Describe the different layers of the atmosphere with a neat labelled diagram showing the temperature variation.
questions.a:
**Diagram**: vertical axis altitude (0-500 km), horizontal axis temperature (°C); a curve falling to −56 °C at the tropopause (11 km), rising to about −2 °C at the stratopause (50 km), falling to about −92 °C at the mesopause (85 km), then rising steeply to ~1200 °C in the thermosphere. Mark the ozone layer at 15-35 km.

1. **Troposphere (0-11 km)**: temperature falls from ~15 °C to −56 °C at about 6.5 °C/km because it is heated from the ground. Contains ~75% of the atmosphere's mass, almost all water vapour, clouds and weather. Major species N$_2$, O$_2$, CO$_2$, H$_2$O.
2. **Stratosphere (11-50 km)**: temperature rises to about −2 °C because ozone absorbs UV radiation ($\mathrm{O_3 + h\nu \rightarrow O_2 + O}$ releases heat). Contains the ozone layer; stable, with little vertical mixing.
3. **Mesosphere (50-85 km)**: temperature falls to about −92 °C, the coldest region; very low ozone; meteors burn up; ions O$_2^+$, NO$^+$.
4. **Thermosphere (85-500 km)**: temperature rises to ~1200 °C as O$_2$ and N$_2$ absorb very short-wavelength UV and X-rays. Contains the ionosphere (O$_2^+$, O$^+$, NO$^+$, free electrons) that reflects radio waves; aurorae occur here.
5. **Exosphere (>500 km)**: outermost, very thin; light gases (H, He) escape to space.

questions.q: Why does temperature increase with altitude in the stratosphere?
questions.a: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs solar UV radiation (200-320 nm). The absorbed energy breaks O$_3$ into O$_2$ + O, and the recombination reactions release heat ($\mathrm{O + O_2 + M \rightarrow O_3 + M}$, where M carries away heat). This heating is greatest in the upper stratosphere, where UV intensity is high, so temperature rises with height.

questions.q: The surface temperature at a place is 30 °C. Using the normal lapse rate, estimate the temperature at 5 km altitude.
questions.a: $T = T_0 - \Gamma z = 30 - 6.5 \times 5 = 30 - 32.5 = -2.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$

questions.q: What is temperature inversion and why is it important in air pollution?
questions.a: Normally temperature falls with height in the troposphere. In an **inversion** a layer of warm air lies above cooler air near the ground (e.g. on clear, calm winter nights when the ground cools by radiation). The cool, dense air below cannot rise, so vertical mixing stops and pollutants are trapped near the surface. This causes severe smog episodes, e.g. London 1952 and Delhi winters.

questions.q: The ozone layer is located in the:
questions.a: The ozone layer lies mainly at 15-35 km, in the stratosphere.

questions.q: The coldest layer of the atmosphere is the:
questions.a: Temperature falls to about −92 °C at the mesopause (~85 km).

questions.q: Radio waves are reflected back to Earth by the:
questions.a: The ionosphere, in the thermosphere, contains free electrons and ions (O₂⁺, NO⁺, O⁺) that reflect radio waves.

topics.why: 'Explain the formation of photochemical smog with reactions' and 'differentiate classical and photochemical smog' are among the most repeated questions in Indian EVS papers.
topics.gist:
**Smog** = smoke + fog. There are two kinds.

**Classical (London, reducing) smog** forms from coal smoke, SO$_2$ and fog in cold, humid weather (London 1952, ~4000 deaths). It is reducing in nature.

**Photochemical (Los Angeles, oxidising) smog** is a brown haze formed when **sunlight** acts on **NO$_x$** and **hydrocarbons (VOCs)** from vehicle exhaust, under warm, dry, calm conditions, often with an inversion.

The chemistry is the exam:
1. Engines make NO at high temperature: $\mathrm{N_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO}$. NO is oxidised: $\mathrm{2NO + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO_2}$.
2. Sunlight splits NO$_2$: $\mathrm{NO_2 + h\nu \rightarrow NO + O}$, and the atomic O makes ozone: $\mathrm{O + O_2 + M \rightarrow O_3 + M}$.
3. Without hydrocarbons, ozone is destroyed again: $\mathrm{O_3 + NO \rightarrow NO_2 + O_2}$ (a null cycle).
4. Hydrocarbons break the null cycle. They are attacked by OH, O and O$_3$ to give peroxy radicals (RO$_2^\bullet$), which convert NO to NO$_2$ *without using ozone*. So O$_3$ accumulates and aldehydes form.
5. Acyl peroxy radicals combine with NO$_2$ to form **PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate)**, $\mathrm{CH_3C(O)OONO_2}$.

The products (O$_3$, PAN, aldehydes such as formaldehyde and acrolein, NO$_2$) are **secondary pollutants**. **Daily cycle**: NO peaks with morning traffic, NO$_2$ an hour or two later, and O$_3$ and PAN at noon to early afternoon when sunlight is strongest.

**Effects**: eye irritation (PAN, acrolein), coughing and asthma, damage to plants (leaf bronzing), cracking of rubber, fading of dyes, poor visibility.

**Control**: catalytic converters, fewer vehicles and cleaner fuels (CNG, BS-VI), less VOC evaporation, free-radical scavengers, and planting NO$_2$-tolerant trees (*Pinus*, *Juniperus*, *Vitis*, *Pyrus*).
key_points: Ingredients: NOₓ + hydrocarbons + sunlight + warm, calm, dry air (inversion).
Formation of NO in engines and its oxidation to NO₂.
NO₂ photolysis and ozone formation; the NO/O₃ null cycle.
Hydrocarbon radicals convert NO to NO₂ without consuming O₃, so O₃ builds up.
PAN formation; PAN, O₃ and aldehydes are secondary pollutants.
Diurnal variation: NO (morning) → NO₂ → O₃/PAN (noon/afternoon).
Effects on humans, plants and materials.
Control measures; differences from classical smog.
formulas: $\mathrm{N_2 + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{high } T} 2NO}$ — in engine cylinders
$\mathrm{2NO + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO_2}$
$\mathrm{NO_2 + h\nu\ (\lambda < 400\ nm) \rightarrow NO + O}$ — primary photochemical step
$\mathrm{O + O_2 + M \rightarrow O_3 + M}$ — ozone formation (M = N₂ or O₂, third body)
$\mathrm{O_3 + NO \rightarrow NO_2 + O_2}$ — null cycle without hydrocarbons
$\mathrm{RH + {}^\bullet OH \rightarrow R^\bullet + H_2O}$;  $\mathrm{R^\bullet + O_2 \rightarrow RO_2^\bullet}$
$\mathrm{RO_2^\bullet + NO \rightarrow RO^\bullet + NO_2}$ — NO to NO₂ without using O₃
$\mathrm{RO^\bullet + O_2 \rightarrow R'CHO + HO_2^\bullet}$;  $\mathrm{HO_2^\bullet + NO \rightarrow {}^\bullet OH + NO_2}$
$\mathrm{CH_3C(O)OO^\bullet + NO_2 \rightarrow CH_3C(O)OONO_2}$ — PAN
traps: Calling photochemical smog 'reducing'. It is OXIDISING (O₃, PAN); London smog is reducing.
Saying photochemical smog occurs on cold foggy winter mornings. It needs strong sunlight: warm, sunny afternoons.
Writing only the NO₂/O₃ reactions. Without the hydrocarbon (radical) step you cannot explain why O₃ accumulates, and that step carries the marks.
Calling ozone a primary pollutant. In smog it is secondary.
Expanding PAN wrongly (it is peroxyacetyl nitrate, not 'polyaromatic nitrogen').
topics.asked_as: 'What is photochemical smog? Explain its formation with chemical reactions, effects and control' (5-10 marks); 'Differentiate between classical and photochemical smog' (5 marks); 'What is PAN?' (2 marks); MCQs on its oxidising nature and timing.

questions.q: What is photochemical smog? Explain its formation with chemical reactions, and give its effects and control measures.
questions.a:
**Photochemical smog** is a brownish, oxidising haze formed by photochemical reactions of nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons (mainly from vehicle exhaust) in the presence of sunlight, under warm, dry and stagnant conditions.

**Formation**
1. $\mathrm{N_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO}$ (high temperature in engines); $\mathrm{2NO + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO_2}$
2. $\mathrm{NO_2 + h\nu \rightarrow NO + O}$
3. $\mathrm{O + O_2 + M \rightarrow O_3 + M}$
4. $\mathrm{O_3 + NO \rightarrow NO_2 + O_2}$ (null cycle: without hydrocarbons O$_3$ stays low)
5. Hydrocarbons are oxidised to radicals: $\mathrm{RH + OH^\bullet \rightarrow R^\bullet + H_2O}$; $\mathrm{R^\bullet + O_2 \rightarrow RO_2^\bullet}$
6. $\mathrm{RO_2^\bullet + NO \rightarrow RO^\bullet + NO_2}$: NO is removed without consuming O$_3$, so ozone accumulates.
7. $\mathrm{RO^\bullet + O_2 \rightarrow RCHO\ (aldehyde) + HO_2^\bullet}$; $\mathrm{HO_2^\bullet + NO \rightarrow OH^\bullet + NO_2}$ (chain continues)
8. $\mathrm{CH_3COO_2^\bullet + NO_2 \rightarrow CH_3COO_2NO_2}$ (PAN)

Products O$_3$, PAN, HCHO, acrolein and NO$_2$ are secondary pollutants; O$_3$ and PAN peak around noon to early afternoon.

**Effects**: eye, nose and throat irritation; aggravates asthma and bronchitis; damages leaves (bronzing, reduced photosynthesis) and crops; cracks rubber, fades dyes, corrodes metals; reduces visibility.

**Control**: (i) catalytic converters to cut NO$_x$ and HC; (ii) cleaner fuels (CNG, BS-VI), better engine design, fewer vehicles, public transport; (iii) control of VOC evaporation from fuel stations and solvents; (iv) free-radical scavengers to stop chain reactions; (v) plants such as *Pinus*, *Juniperus*, *Pyrus*, *Vitis* that metabolise NO$_2$.

questions.q: Differentiate between classical (London) smog and photochemical (Los Angeles) smog.
questions.a:
| Classical smog | Photochemical smog |
|---|---|
| Smoke + SO$_2$ + fog | NO$_x$ + hydrocarbons + sunlight |
| Reducing in nature | Oxidising in nature |
| Cold, humid weather; winter, early morning | Warm, sunny, dry weather; summer, noon/afternoon |
| Source: coal burning | Source: vehicle exhaust |
| Main pollutants: SO$_2$, soot, H$_2$SO$_4$ droplets | O$_3$, PAN, aldehydes, NO$_2$ |
| Effects: bronchitis, lung disease | Eye irritation, asthma, plant damage, rubber cracking |
| Example: London 1952 | Los Angeles 1940s; Delhi summers |

questions.q: What is PAN? How is it formed and what are its effects?
questions.a: PAN is **peroxyacetyl nitrate**, $\mathrm{CH_3C(O)OONO_2}$, a secondary pollutant of photochemical smog. It forms when acetyl peroxy radicals (from oxidation of hydrocarbons/aldehydes) combine with NO$_2$: $\mathrm{CH_3C(O)OO^\bullet + NO_2 \rightarrow CH_3C(O)OONO_2}$. It is a strong eye irritant (lachrymator), damages plant leaves and is a reservoir that transports NO$_x$ over long distances.

questions.q: Explain why ozone concentration in a city peaks around noon while NO peaks in the early morning.
questions.a: In the morning rush hour vehicles emit NO, so NO peaks first. NO is oxidised to NO$_2$ over the next hour or two, so NO$_2$ peaks next. As sunlight intensifies towards midday, NO$_2$ is photolysed ($\mathrm{NO_2 + h\nu \rightarrow NO + O}$) and the O atoms form O$_3$. Hydrocarbon peroxy radicals keep converting NO back to NO$_2$ without consuming ozone, so O$_3$ (and PAN) build up and peak at noon to early afternoon, then fall in the evening as sunlight fades.

questions.q: Photochemical smog is:
options: Reducing in nature and formed in winter mornings
Oxidising in nature and formed on sunny days
Reducing in nature and formed on sunny days
questions.a: It contains oxidants such as O₃ and PAN and needs sunlight, so it forms on warm sunny days.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of photochemical smog?
options: Sulphur dioxide as the main constituent
questions.a: SO₂ is the main constituent of classical (London) smog, not photochemical smog.

questions.q: The primary photochemical reaction that initiates photochemical smog is:
questions.a: Photolysis of NO₂ by sunlight gives atomic oxygen, which forms ozone and starts the chain.

topics.topic: Sources and effects of air pollutants
topics.why: 'Describe the causes, effects and control measures of air pollution' is the archetypal 10-mark EVS question; a table of pollutant, source and effect scores well.
topics.gist:
**Air pollution** is the presence in the atmosphere of one or more contaminants (gases, particles) in quantities and for durations that harm humans, animals, plants or materials. The Air Act 1981 has its own legal definition.

**Classification**: **primary pollutants** are emitted directly (CO, SO$_2$, NO, hydrocarbons, particulates). **Secondary pollutants** form in the air by reactions (O$_3$, PAN, H$_2$SO$_4$, HNO$_3$, sulphate aerosols). Sources are **natural** (volcanoes, forest fires, dust storms, pollen, marsh CH$_4$) or **anthropogenic**: vehicles, thermal power plants, industries, burning of crop residue and waste, domestic chulhas, construction dust, mining.

**Major pollutants and effects**:
- **CO** (incomplete combustion, vehicles) binds haemoglobin about 200-250 times more strongly than O$_2$, forming carboxyhaemoglobin. It causes headache, dizziness and, at high levels, death.
- **SO$_2$** (coal and oil burning, smelters) irritates the respiratory tract and causes **acid rain** (pH < 5.6), which corrodes buildings ('marble cancer' of the Taj Mahal) and damages forests and lakes.
- **NO$_x$** (vehicles, power plants) irritate the lungs, cause acid rain and drive photochemical smog.
- **Hydrocarbons/VOCs** contribute to smog; benzene is carcinogenic.
- **Particulate matter** (PM$_{10}$, PM$_{2.5}$) penetrates deep into the lungs, causing asthma, heart disease and lung cancer, and reduces visibility.
- **Lead** from old leaded petrol and smelters is neurotoxic.
- **CO$_2$, CH$_4$, N$_2$O** cause global warming; **CFCs** deplete ozone.

The **Bhopal gas tragedy** (2-3 December 1984, methyl isocyanate leak from Union Carbide, thousands dead) is the case study MANIT students should know. India's **NAAQS (2009)** cover 12 pollutants, and the **AQI** has six bands from Good (0-50) to Severe (401-500).
key_points: Definition of air pollution.
Primary vs secondary pollutants with examples; natural vs anthropogenic sources.
For each of CO, SOₓ, NOₓ, HC, PM, Pb, O₃: source and effect.
Acid rain: formation reactions and effects (pH < 5.6).
CO toxicity: carboxyhaemoglobin, affinity ~200-250× O₂.
Indoor air pollution: chulha smoke, radon, formaldehyde, tobacco.
Bhopal gas tragedy 1984 (MIC).
NAAQS 2009 (12 pollutants) and AQI categories; general control measures.
formulas: $\mathrm{Hb + CO \rightleftharpoons HbCO}$ — carboxyhaemoglobin (affinity ~200-250× that of O₂)
$\mathrm{2SO_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2H_2SO_4}$ — acid rain (sulphuric)
$\mathrm{4NO_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4HNO_3}$ — acid rain (nitric)
$\mathrm{CaCO_3 + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CaSO_4 + H_2O + CO_2}$ — 'marble cancer' (Taj Mahal)
$C\,(\mu\mathrm{g/m^3}) = \dfrac{C\,(\mathrm{ppm}) \times M \times 1000}{24.45}$ — ppm to µg/m³ at 25 °C, 1 atm

Writing that natural rain has pH 7. Natural rain is ~5.6 (dissolved CO₂); acid rain is below 5.6.
Saying CO 'causes acid rain'. CO is not acidic; acid rain comes from SO₂ and NOₓ.

questions.q: Define air pollution. Describe the sources and effects of the major air pollutants.
questions.a:
**Air pollution**: presence of solid, liquid or gaseous substances in the atmosphere in concentrations that are harmful to humans, other living beings, property or the environment.

**Sources**: *Natural*: volcanoes, forest fires, dust storms, pollen, sea spray, marshes. *Anthropogenic*: vehicles, thermal power plants, industries (cement, steel, fertiliser, refinery), domestic burning of wood/coal/dung, crop-residue burning, construction and road dust, mining, waste burning.

| Pollutant | Main source | Effects |
|---|---|---|
| CO | incomplete combustion, vehicles | forms carboxyhaemoglobin; headache, dizziness, death at high levels |
| SO$_2$ | coal/oil burning, smelters | respiratory irritation; acid rain; damage to plants (chlorosis) and buildings |
| NO$_x$ | vehicles, power plants | lung irritation; acid rain; photochemical smog |
| Hydrocarbons/VOCs | vehicles, solvents, fuel evaporation | smog formation; benzene is carcinogenic |
| Particulate matter (PM$_{10}$, PM$_{2.5}$) | combustion, dust, industries | asthma, bronchitis, heart disease, lung cancer; poor visibility; soiling |
| Lead | smelters, batteries, old petrol | brain and kidney damage, anaemia, low IQ in children |
| O$_3$ (secondary) | photochemical reactions | eye irritation, lung damage, crop loss |
| CO$_2$, CH$_4$, N$_2$O | fuels, agriculture | global warming |
| CFCs | refrigerants, aerosols | stratospheric ozone depletion |

**Effects on materials**: corrosion of metals, erosion of marble and limestone, fading of dyes, cracking of rubber. **On plants**: chlorosis, necrosis, reduced growth.

**Control (brief)**: cleaner fuels, catalytic converters, ESPs and scrubbers in industry, tall stacks with green belts, public transport, enforcement of the Air Act 1981 and NAAQS.

questions.q: Differentiate between primary and secondary air pollutants with examples.
questions.a: **Primary pollutants** are emitted directly from a source in harmful form, e.g. CO, SO$_2$, NO, hydrocarbons, particulates. **Secondary pollutants** are formed in the atmosphere by chemical reactions among primary pollutants and natural constituents, e.g. O$_3$, PAN, H$_2$SO$_4$, HNO$_3$, sulphate aerosols.

questions.q: What is acid rain? Explain its formation and effects.
questions.a:
**Acid rain** is precipitation with pH less than 5.6 (normal rain is ~5.6 because of dissolved CO$_2$), caused by SO$_2$ and NO$_x$ emissions.

**Formation**: $\mathrm{2SO_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2SO_3}$; $\mathrm{SO_3 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_4}$; $\mathrm{4NO_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4HNO_3}$. The acids are carried by wind and deposited as wet (rain, snow, fog) or dry deposition.

**Effects**: (i) acidification of lakes, killing fish; (ii) leaching of nutrients and release of toxic Al$^{3+}$ in soils, damaging forests; (iii) corrosion of metals and erosion of marble and limestone: $\mathrm{CaCO_3 + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CaSO_4 + H_2O + CO_2}$ (Taj Mahal yellowing from the Mathura refinery and industries); (iv) respiratory problems; (v) leaching of heavy metals into drinking water.

**Control**: low-sulphur fuels, flue-gas desulphurisation, catalytic converters, liming of lakes.

questions.q: Convert 0.1 ppm of SO₂ to µg/m³ at 25 °C and 1 atm (M of SO₂ = 64).
questions.a:
$C = \dfrac{0.1 \times 64 \times 1000}{24.45} = \dfrac{6400}{24.45} \approx 262\ \mu\mathrm{g/m^3}$

(This is well above the Indian 24-hour NAAQS of 80 µg/m³.)

questions.q: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous even at low concentrations?
questions.a: CO combines with haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin (HbCO); its affinity for Hb is about 200-250 times that of O$_2$. So even small concentrations block oxygen transport to tissues. It is colourless and odourless, so it is not noticed. Symptoms: headache, dizziness, impaired judgement, unconsciousness and death at high levels (e.g. from a charcoal stove in a closed room).

questions.q: The gas responsible for the Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984 was:
questions.a: Methyl isocyanate (MIC, CH₃NCO) leaked from the Union Carbide pesticide plant on the night of 2-3 December 1984.

questions.q: Rain is called acid rain when its pH is less than:
questions.a: Unpolluted rain is about pH 5.6 because CO₂ dissolves to form carbonic acid; below 5.6 is acid rain.

topics.why: 'Explain ozone layer depletion by CFCs with reactions; effects and remedies' is asked almost every year; the Chapman and Cl-catalytic cycle equations are expected.
topics.gist:
**Stratospheric ozone** (15-35 km) absorbs harmful **UV-B (280-315 nm)** and UV-C radiation. Its amount is measured in **Dobson Units** (1 DU = 0.01 mm thickness of pure O$_3$ at STP). The normal value is about 300 DU; an 'ozone hole' is a region below 220 DU.

**Natural balance (Chapman cycle)**: O$_2$ is split by UV (<242 nm), the O atoms form O$_3$, and O$_3$ absorbs UV and is split again. Production and destruction balance each other.

**Depletion by CFCs**: chlorofluorocarbons (CFC-11 CFCl$_3$, CFC-12 CF$_2$Cl$_2$), used in refrigerators, ACs, aerosol sprays and foams, are inert in the troposphere and drift up over years. In the stratosphere UV releases **Cl atoms**, which destroy ozone **catalytically**: Cl + O$_3$ → ClO + O$_2$, then ClO + O → Cl + O$_2$. The Cl is regenerated, so **one Cl atom can destroy about 10$^5$ O$_3$ molecules**. Halons release Br, which is even more effective. NO from supersonic aircraft and N$_2$O also destroy O$_3$ catalytically.

**Antarctic ozone hole** (spring, September-October): in the polar winter vortex, **polar stratospheric clouds** form at about −80 °C. On their ice surfaces the inactive reservoirs HCl and ClONO$_2$ react to give Cl$_2$, which sunlight splits into Cl atoms when spring arrives, causing rapid destruction.

**Effects of more UV-B**: skin cancer, cataract, weaker immunity, reduced crop yields and phytoplankton (the base of marine food chains), and degradation of plastics.

**Remedies**: the **Vienna Convention 1985**, the **Montreal Protocol 1987** (phase-out of CFCs, halons, CCl$_4$), and the **Kigali Amendment 2016** (HFCs). Substitutes are HCFCs (interim), HFCs and hydrocarbons. India's ODS Rules date from 2000. World Ozone Day is 16 September. The ozone layer is now slowly recovering.
key_points: Role of the ozone layer: absorbs UV-B/UV-C; location 15-35 km.
Dobson Unit; normal ~300 DU; hole < 220 DU.
Chapman cycle (formation and natural destruction) with equations.
CFC photolysis and the Cl/ClO catalytic cycle; one Cl destroys ~10⁵ O₃.
Other ozone-depleting substances: halons (Br), CCl₄, methyl chloroform, N₂O/NO.
Antarctic ozone hole: polar vortex, PSCs, HCl + ClONO₂ → Cl₂, spring sunlight.
Effects of UV-B on humans, plants, aquatic life, materials.
Montreal Protocol 1987, Vienna 1985, Kigali 2016; substitutes.
formulas: $\mathrm{O_2 + h\nu\ (\lambda < 242\ nm) \rightarrow 2O}$;  $\mathrm{O + O_2 + M \rightarrow O_3 + M}$ — ozone formation (Chapman)
$\mathrm{O_3 + h\nu\ (\lambda = 200\text{-}320\ nm) \rightarrow O_2 + O}$;  $\mathrm{O + O_3 \rightarrow 2O_2}$ — natural destruction
$\mathrm{CF_2Cl_2 + h\nu \rightarrow {}^\bullet CF_2Cl + Cl^\bullet}$ — photolysis of CFC-12
$\mathrm{Cl^\bullet + O_3 \rightarrow ClO^\bullet + O_2}$;  $\mathrm{ClO^\bullet + O \rightarrow Cl^\bullet + O_2}$;  net $\mathrm{O_3 + O \rightarrow 2O_2}$
$\mathrm{NO + O_3 \rightarrow NO_2 + O_2}$;  $\mathrm{NO_2 + O \rightarrow NO + O_2}$ — NOₓ catalytic cycle
$\mathrm{ClONO_2 + HCl \xrightarrow{PSC} Cl_2 + HNO_3}$;  $\mathrm{Cl_2 + h\nu \rightarrow 2Cl^\bullet}$ — Antarctic spring activation
$1\ \mathrm{DU} = 0.01\ \mathrm{mm}$ of pure O₃ at STP
traps: Confusing ozone depletion with global warming. They are different problems, though CFCs also happen to be greenhouse gases.
Saying CFCs react with ozone directly. CFCs must first be photolysed to release Cl atoms; Cl is the catalyst.
Placing the hole in the Arctic or in summer. It is mainly over Antarctica in its spring (September-October).
Writing Kyoto Protocol (1997, greenhouse gases) instead of Montreal Protocol (1987, ozone).
Forgetting to write the 'net' reaction and the regeneration of Cl, which is the point of 'catalytic'.
Thinking 'good' stratospheric ozone and 'bad' tropospheric (smog) ozone are the same issue.
