questions.q: What is ozone layer depletion? Explain the mechanism of ozone depletion by CFCs with reactions, and discuss its effects and control measures.
questions.a:
**Ozone depletion** is the thinning of the stratospheric ozone layer, mainly by man-made chlorine- and bromine-containing compounds, so that more UV-B reaches the Earth.

**Natural balance (Chapman cycle)**
$\mathrm{O_2 + h\nu \rightarrow 2O}$; $\mathrm{O + O_2 + M \rightarrow O_3 + M}$; $\mathrm{O_3 + h\nu \rightarrow O_2 + O}$; $\mathrm{O + O_3 \rightarrow 2O_2}$

**Mechanism with CFCs**
1. CFCs are inert, insoluble and long-lived (50-100 years), so they reach the stratosphere.
2. UV photolysis: $\mathrm{CF_2Cl_2 + h\nu \rightarrow CF_2Cl^\bullet + Cl^\bullet}$ (and $\mathrm{CFCl_3 + h\nu \rightarrow CFCl_2^\bullet + Cl^\bullet}$)
3. $\mathrm{Cl^\bullet + O_3 \rightarrow ClO^\bullet + O_2}$
4. $\mathrm{ClO^\bullet + O \rightarrow Cl^\bullet + O_2}$
5. Net: $\mathrm{O_3 + O \rightarrow 2O_2}$. Cl is regenerated, so one Cl atom destroys about $10^5$ O$_3$ molecules before it is locked up as HCl or ClONO$_2$.

Similarly NO: $\mathrm{NO + O_3 \rightarrow NO_2 + O_2}$; $\mathrm{NO_2 + O \rightarrow NO + O_2}$. Halons release Br, which is even more destructive.

**Antarctic hole**: in the polar winter, polar stratospheric clouds form; on them $\mathrm{HCl + ClONO_2 \rightarrow Cl_2 + HNO_3}$; in spring sunlight $\mathrm{Cl_2 \rightarrow 2Cl}$ and ozone falls sharply (below 220 DU).

**Effects of increased UV-B**: skin cancer (melanoma), sunburn, cataract, suppression of the immune system; reduced crop yield and photosynthesis; damage to phytoplankton and fish larvae, upsetting marine food chains; degradation of paints and plastics; contribution to warming.

**Control**: Vienna Convention (1985), Montreal Protocol (1987) to phase out CFCs, halons, CCl$_4$ and methyl chloroform; Kigali Amendment (2016) to phase down HFCs; substitutes: HCFCs (interim), HFCs, hydrocarbons (isobutane), ammonia; recovery and recycling of refrigerants; India's ODS (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000.

questions.q: What is a Dobson Unit? What is meant by the 'ozone hole'?
questions.a: A Dobson Unit is the measure of total ozone in a vertical column: 1 DU = a layer of pure ozone 0.01 mm thick at STP. The normal value is about 300 DU (i.e. 3 mm). The **ozone hole** is a region (mainly over Antarctica in September-October) where total column ozone falls below 220 DU.

questions.q: Explain why the ozone hole forms over Antarctica in spring.
questions.a: During the polar winter a strong vortex isolates very cold air (below about −80 °C), and polar stratospheric clouds (PSCs) of ice and nitric acid form. On PSC surfaces the inactive chlorine reservoirs react: $\mathrm{HCl + ClONO_2 \rightarrow Cl_2 + HNO_3}$; HNO$_3$ stays in the ice, removing NO$_x$ that would otherwise lock up Cl. When sunlight returns in spring (September-October), $\mathrm{Cl_2 + h\nu \rightarrow 2Cl}$ releases large amounts of active Cl, which rapidly destroys ozone by the catalytic cycle. When the vortex breaks up in late spring, ozone-rich air flows in and the hole closes.

questions.q: Write a short note on the Montreal Protocol.
questions.a: The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer was signed in 1987 (in force 1989) under the Vienna Convention (1985). It set time-bound phase-outs of CFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform, HCFCs and methyl bromide, with a fund to help developing countries (India joined in 1992). The Kigali Amendment (2016) adds a phase-down of HFCs, which are greenhouse gases. It is regarded as the most successful environmental treaty: ODS levels are falling and the ozone layer is expected to recover around mid-century.

questions.q: One chlorine atom released from a CFC can destroy approximately how many ozone molecules?
questions.a: Because Cl is regenerated in the ClO/Cl cycle it acts as a catalyst, destroying around 10⁵ O₃ molecules before it is removed.

questions.q: The international treaty to phase out ozone-depleting substances is the:
questions.a: Montreal Protocol (1987). Kyoto and Paris deal with greenhouse gases.

questions.q: The stratospheric ozone layer mainly protects us from:
questions.a: Ozone absorbs UV-B (280-315 nm) and UV-C; increased UV-B causes skin cancer and cataract.

topics.topic: Control of gaseous and particulate pollutants
topics.why: 'Explain the working of an electrostatic precipitator / cyclone separator with a diagram' and 'methods for control of gaseous pollutants' are standard 5-10 mark questions.
topics.gist:
Control starts at the **source**: cleaner fuels (low-sulphur coal, CNG, LPG), process changes, good maintenance, energy efficiency and relocating industries. After that come **end-of-pipe devices**. Dispersal through tall stacks only dilutes pollutants; it is not removal.

**Particulate control devices** (in order of the smallest particle they remove):
- **Gravity settling chamber**: gas slows down and particles >50 µm settle (Stokes' law). Cheap, low efficiency.
- **Cyclone separator**: gas enters tangentially and spins, centrifugal force throws particles (>5-10 µm) to the wall, they slide to the hopper and clean gas leaves through the central outlet. Efficiency 50-90%.
- **Fabric (bag) filter**: gas passes through woven or felt bags and dust cake builds up (down to ~0.1 µm, >99%). Limited by temperature and moisture.
- **Wet scrubber** (spray tower, venturi): water droplets capture particles and soluble gases together.
- **Electrostatic precipitator (ESP)**: a high DC voltage (30-100 kV) between discharge wires and earthed collecting plates creates a **corona**. Particles pick up negative charge, migrate to the plates and are removed by rapping. Efficiency >99% down to ~0.1 µm with low pressure drop. It is the standard device in thermal power plants and cement works.

**Gaseous pollutant control**:
- **Absorption** in a liquid, e.g. SO$_2$ by lime/limestone slurry (**flue-gas desulphurisation**, which gives gypsum).
- **Adsorption** on activated carbon, silica gel or zeolites (VOCs, odours).
- **Combustion/incineration** (flares, thermal or catalytic oxidisers) for hydrocarbons and CO.
- **Catalytic converters** in vehicles: a three-way Pt/Pd/Rh catalyst converts CO, HC and NO$_x$ to CO$_2$, H$_2$O and N$_2$.
- **Condensation** of high-concentration vapours. Selective catalytic reduction with NH$_3$ removes NO$_x$.

Supporting measures: adequate stack height (CPCB formula), green belts, and enforcement of standards.
key_points: Hierarchy: source control first, then collection devices, then dispersion (not true control).
Settling chamber, cyclone, bag filter, wet scrubber, ESP: principle, particle size range, efficiency, use.
ESP: corona discharge, particle charging, migration to collecting plates, rapping; >99%.
Gaseous control: absorption, adsorption, combustion, catalytic conversion, condensation.
FGD reactions with limestone; catalytic converter reactions.
Efficiency of devices in series.
Stack height and green belt as supporting measures.
formulas: $v_t = \dfrac{g d^2 (\rho_p - \rho_g)}{18\mu}$ — Stokes' settling velocity (gravity settling chambers)
$\eta = 1 - e^{-wA/Q}$ — Deutsch-Anderson equation for ESP efficiency ($w$ drift velocity, $A$ plate area, $Q$ gas flow)
$\eta_{overall} = 1 - (1-\eta_1)(1-\eta_2)$ — devices in series
$\mathrm{SO_2 + CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaSO_3 + CO_2}$;  $\mathrm{CaSO_3 + \tfrac12 O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O}$ — wet limestone FGD (gypsum)
$\mathrm{2CO + O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2}$;  $\mathrm{2NO + 2CO \rightarrow N_2 + 2CO_2}$;  $\mathrm{C_xH_y + (x + y/4)O_2 \rightarrow xCO_2 + \tfrac{y}{2}H_2O}$ — three-way catalytic converter
$\mathrm{4NO + 4NH_3 + O_2 \rightarrow 4N_2 + 6H_2O}$ — selective catalytic reduction
$H = 14\,Q^{0.3}$ — CPCB minimum stack height in m ($Q$ = SO₂ emission in kg/h; minimum 30 m)
traps: Saying a cyclone removes fine particles efficiently. It is poor below ~5 µm; ESPs or bag filters are used for fines.
Mixing up absorption (gas dissolves INTO a liquid) with adsorption (gas held ON a solid surface).
Calling tall chimneys a control method. They disperse, not remove, pollutants.
Drawing an ESP without labelling discharge electrode, collecting plates, hopper, and the HV DC supply.
Saying a catalytic converter works with leaded petrol. Lead poisons the catalyst.

questions.q: Explain the principle and working of an electrostatic precipitator (ESP) with a neat diagram. Give its merits and demerits.
questions.a:
**Principle**: particles in a gas are given an electric charge by a corona discharge and are then attracted to an oppositely charged (earthed) collecting surface.

**Diagram (describe and label)**: a duct or chamber with vertical earthed collecting plates (or a tube) and thin discharge wires hung between them, connected to a high-voltage negative DC supply (30-100 kV); dirty gas inlet, clean gas outlet, rappers, and a dust hopper at the bottom.

**Working**
1. The high voltage creates a corona around the wires; gas molecules ionise, producing negative ions and electrons.
2. Ions attach to the dust particles, which become negatively charged.
3. Charged particles migrate under the electric field to the earthed collecting plates and are neutralised.
4. Plates are periodically rapped (or washed in wet ESPs); the dust falls into the hopper.
5. Clean gas leaves from the outlet.

**Merits**: efficiency >99% even for 0.1-1 µm particles; handles large gas volumes at high temperature; low pressure drop and running cost; dry dust can be recovered (fly ash for cement).

**Demerits**: high capital cost and large space; not for gaseous pollutants; efficiency depends on dust resistivity; risk with explosive dusts; high-voltage safety needed.

**Uses**: thermal power plants, cement kilns, steel plants.

questions.q: Describe the working of a cyclone separator.
questions.a: A cyclone is a cylindrical vessel with a conical bottom. Dust-laden gas enters tangentially at the top and is forced into a downward spiral (outer vortex). Centrifugal force throws heavier particles outward to the wall, where they lose velocity and slide down to the dust hopper at the cone's apex. Near the bottom the gas reverses and rises in an inner vortex, leaving through the central vortex-finder outlet at the top. It removes particles larger than about 5-10 µm with 50-90% efficiency, has no moving parts, low cost and works at high temperature; it is poor for fine particles and is often used as a pre-cleaner before an ESP or bag filter.

questions.q: Discuss the methods used to control gaseous air pollutants.
questions.a:
1. **Absorption**: polluted gas is contacted with a liquid in which the pollutant dissolves or reacts (packed towers, spray towers). E.g. SO$_2$ in lime/limestone slurry: $\mathrm{SO_2 + CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaSO_3 + CO_2}$, oxidised to gypsum; NH$_3$ in water; HCl in water.
2. **Adsorption**: pollutant molecules are held on the surface of a porous solid (activated carbon, silica gel, alumina, zeolites); used for VOCs, solvent vapours and odours; the adsorbent is regenerated by steam.
3. **Combustion (incineration)**: combustible gases (HC, CO, odorous compounds) are burnt to CO$_2$ and H$_2$O in flares, thermal incinerators or catalytic incinerators (lower temperature).
4. **Catalytic conversion**: three-way catalytic converter (Pt, Pd, Rh) in vehicles: $\mathrm{2CO + O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2}$; $\mathrm{2NO + 2CO \rightarrow N_2 + 2CO_2}$; hydrocarbons oxidised to CO$_2$ + H$_2$O. Industrial NO$_x$ by selective catalytic reduction with NH$_3$.
5. **Condensation**: cooling to condense high-concentration vapours for recovery.
6. **Source modification**: low-sulphur fuels, fuel switching (CNG), low-NO$_x$ burners, process change.

questions.q: A cyclone with 80% efficiency is followed by an ESP with 99% efficiency. What is the overall collection efficiency?
An ESP has a collecting area of 5000 m², gas flow 200 m³/s and drift velocity 0.1 m/s. Find its efficiency.
Which device is most efficient for removing sub-micron particulate matter from flue gases of a thermal power plant?
questions.a: ESPs collect particles down to about 0.1 µm with >99% efficiency; settling chambers and cyclones only handle coarse particles.

questions.q: Removal of VOCs by passing gas through a bed of activated carbon is an example of:
questions.a: Molecules are held on the solid surface of carbon: adsorption. Absorption means dissolving into a liquid.

Hydrological cycle: evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff (diagram).
Unique properties of water and their environmental significance.
Uses and importance of water.

$P = E + R + \Delta S$ — water balance (precipitation = evapotranspiration + runoff + change in storage)

questions.q: Explain the hydrological cycle with a labelled diagram.
questions.a:
**Diagram**: sun; ocean and land at the bottom; arrows for evaporation from the ocean and transpiration from plants rising to clouds; condensation in clouds; precipitation (rain, snow) falling on land and sea; surface runoff to rivers back to the sea; infiltration and percolation to groundwater; groundwater flow to rivers and sea; snow and ice storage.

**Processes**
1. **Evaporation**: solar heat converts water from oceans, lakes and soil into vapour.
2. **Transpiration**: plants release water vapour through stomata (together: evapotranspiration).
3. **Condensation**: rising vapour cools and condenses on dust nuclei to form clouds.
4. **Precipitation**: water returns as rain, snow or hail.
5. **Infiltration/percolation**: part soaks into soil and recharges aquifers.
6. **Runoff**: excess flows over land into streams and rivers, back to the sea.
7. **Storage**: in oceans, ice caps, lakes, groundwater.

The cycle is driven by solar energy and gravity, distributes fresh water and heat, and naturally purifies water.

questions.q: List the properties of water that make it important for life and the environment.
questions.a:
1. **High specific heat** (4.18 J/g K): oceans and water bodies moderate climate; body temperature is stable.
2. **High latent heat of vaporisation**: evaporative cooling (sweating, transpiration); heat transport in the atmosphere.
3. **Maximum density at 4 °C**: ice floats and insulates water below, so aquatic life survives winter.
4. **High dielectric constant / universal solvent**: dissolves and transports nutrients in soil, plants and blood.
5. **High surface tension and capillarity**: water rises in soil and plant xylem.
6. **Transparency**: light reaches aquatic plants for photosynthesis.

questions.q: The atmosphere holds about 13,000 km³ of water and global precipitation is about 505,000 km³ per year. Estimate the residence time of water in the atmosphere.
questions.a: $\tau = \dfrac{V}{Q} = \dfrac{13{,}000}{505{,}000} = 0.0257$ year $\approx 0.0257 \times 365 \approx 9.4$ days.

questions.q: Define hydrosphere.
questions.a: The hydrosphere is the total water of the Earth in all its forms and locations: oceans, seas, rivers, lakes, ponds, glaciers and ice caps, groundwater, soil moisture and atmospheric water vapour. It covers about 71% of the Earth's surface.

questions.q: Water has maximum density at:
questions.a: At 4 °C. So ice (less dense) floats and lakes freeze from the top.

questions.q: The largest store of fresh water on Earth is:
questions.a: Roughly 69% of fresh water is frozen in ice caps and glaciers; groundwater holds about 30%.

topics.why: A favourite 2-mark 'differentiate with examples' and a part of every 'sources of water pollution' long answer.
topics.gist:
**Water pollution** is any physical, chemical or biological change in water quality that harms living organisms or makes water unfit for its intended use.

Sources are classified by **how the pollution enters** the water body.

**Point sources** discharge pollutants at a **specific, identifiable location**, usually through a pipe, drain or outfall. Examples: an industrial effluent outfall, a sewage treatment plant or municipal drain, a thermal power plant's hot-water discharge, an oil-tanker spill. They are easy to locate, measure, regulate (consent under the Water Act 1974) and treat at the end of the pipe.

**Non-point (diffuse) sources** release pollutants **over a large area** with no single discharge point. Rain picks up pollutants and carries them in runoff or seepage. Examples: agricultural runoff carrying fertilisers (N, P) and pesticides, urban stormwater with oil, metals and litter, construction and mining sites eroding sediment, animal waste from grazing land, atmospheric deposition (acid rain), and septic-tank seepage. They are intermittent, weather-dependent, hard to trace and monitor, and are controlled by **best management practices** rather than treatment plants.

In India, untreated urban sewage is the biggest point source and farm runoff is the biggest non-point source. Groundwater is polluted by both: leaking tanks and injection wells (point), and fertiliser leaching and landfill leachate (diffuse).
key_points: Definition of water pollution.
Point source: identifiable single outlet; examples.
Non-point source: diffuse, large area, runoff-driven; examples.
Differences: identification, measurement, regulation, treatment, variability.
Control of point sources: treatment (STP, ETP), consent, standards.
Control of non-point sources: buffer strips, reduced fertiliser use, contour farming, wetlands, stormwater management.
traps: Calling agricultural runoff a point source because it enters at a 'point' of the river. It is diffuse.
Giving only examples without the defining idea (single identifiable outlet vs diffuse area).
Saying non-point pollution is minor. It is the main cause of eutrophication in many lakes.

questions.q: Differentiate between point and non-point sources of water pollution with examples.
questions.a:
| Point source | Non-point source |
|---|---|
| Discharges at a specific, identifiable location (pipe, drain, outfall) | Diffuse; pollutants enter over a wide area via runoff and seepage |
| Easy to locate, measure and monitor | Difficult to trace and quantify |
| Fairly continuous discharge | Intermittent, depends on rainfall |
| Controlled by end-of-pipe treatment and discharge consent | Controlled by land-use and best management practices |
| Examples: industrial effluent outfall, sewage drain, STP discharge, thermal plant outlet | Examples: agricultural runoff (fertilisers, pesticides), urban stormwater, construction-site sediment, acid rain |

questions.q: Discuss the major sources of water pollution.
questions.a:
**Point sources**
1. Domestic sewage from towns: organic matter, pathogens, detergents; the largest source in India.
2. Industrial effluents: tanneries (Cr), distilleries, paper mills, textile dyes, chemical and pharmaceutical units, heavy metals, acids.
3. Thermal and nuclear power plants: hot water (thermal pollution), radioactive waste.
4. Oil spills from tankers and offshore rigs.

**Non-point sources**
1. Agricultural runoff: fertilisers (N, P), pesticides, sediment, animal waste.
2. Urban stormwater: oil, grease, heavy metals, litter.
3. Mining and construction sites: sediment, acid mine drainage.
4. Landfill leachate and septic-tank seepage into groundwater.
5. Atmospheric deposition (acid rain, mercury).
6. Religious and cultural practices: idol immersion, bathing, dumping of flowers and ashes.

questions.q: Suggest three methods to control non-point source pollution from agriculture.
questions.a:
1. **Vegetated buffer strips** along streams to trap sediment and absorb nutrients.
2. **Balanced, need-based fertiliser and pesticide use** (soil testing, IPM, slow-release fertilisers, organic manure).
3. **Soil conservation practices**: contour ploughing, terracing, cover crops to reduce runoff.
(Also: constructed wetlands, controlled irrigation, fencing animals away from water.)

questions.q: Define water pollution.
questions.a: Water pollution is the alteration of the physical, chemical or biological characteristics of water by the addition of substances or energy (heat) that makes it harmful to living organisms or unfit for drinking, agriculture, industry or recreation.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-point source of water pollution?
options: Effluent pipe of a paper mill
Outfall of a sewage treatment plant
Cooling-water outlet of a thermal power station
questions.a: Agricultural runoff enters over a wide area with no single outlet; the others are point sources.

questions.q: Point sources of pollution are generally easier to control because they:
options: Can be located and treated at a specific outlet
questions.a: A single identifiable discharge can be monitored, given a consent and treated before release.

topics.topic: Classification and effects of water pollutants
topics.why: The 'causes and effects' half of the classic 10-mark water pollution question; eutrophication and heavy-metal diseases (Minamata, itai-itai) are frequent short notes.
topics.gist:
Water pollutants are classified by their nature and effect.

1. **Oxygen-demanding wastes** (biodegradable organic matter from sewage, food, dairy, paper and sugar industries). Bacteria decompose them and use up dissolved oxygen (high **BOD**), so fish die and the water turns anaerobic and foul (H$_2$S, CH$_4$).
2. **Disease-causing agents** (pathogens from faeces): cholera, typhoid, dysentery, hepatitis A, polio, jaundice, diarrhoea. Indicator: coliform bacteria.
3. **Plant nutrients** (nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers, detergents and sewage) cause **eutrophication**: algal bloom, death and decay of the algae, DO crash, fish kill. Excess nitrate causes blue-baby syndrome.
4. **Toxic inorganic chemicals**: acids and alkalis, and **heavy metals**. Mercury causes **Minamata disease** (Japan, 1950s, methylmercury in fish). Cadmium causes **itai-itai** (bone softening, Japan). Arsenic causes arsenicosis and skin cancer (West Bengal, Bangladesh). Lead causes plumbism. Excess fluoride (>1.5 mg/L) causes dental and skeletal fluorosis (Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh and parts of MP). Hexavalent chromium (tanneries) is carcinogenic.
5. **Organic chemicals**: pesticides (DDT, endosulfan, which biomagnify), detergents (foam, phosphate), phenols, oils and PCBs.
6. **Sediments and suspended solids** cause turbidity, block light and smother spawning beds.
7. **Oil spills** form a film that stops oxygen transfer and coats birds' feathers.
8. **Radioactive substances** (mining, nuclear plants, hospitals).
9. **Heat** (thermal pollution), which lowers DO.

Persistent pollutants show **bioaccumulation** and **biomagnification**. Effects extend from health to ecosystems (loss of biodiversity) and the economy (fisheries, tourism, treatment cost).
key_points: Classification: oxygen-demanding, pathogens, nutrients, inorganic/heavy metals, organic chemicals, sediments, oil, radioactive, thermal.
Effect of organic waste on DO and BOD.
Water-borne diseases and coliform indicator.
Eutrophication: sequence of steps and consequences.
Heavy metals and diseases: Hg-Minamata, Cd-itai-itai, As-arsenicosis, F-fluorosis, Pb-plumbism, NO₃⁻-blue baby.
Biomagnification of persistent pollutants.
Effects of oil spills and suspended solids.

$\mathrm{Hg^{2+} \xrightarrow{\text{bacteria}} CH_3Hg^+}$ — microbial methylation of mercury (fat-soluble, biomagnifies)

Describing eutrophication as 'nutrients poison fish'. Fish die from oxygen depletion when algae decay.
Saying fluoride is always harmful. Up to 1 mg/L prevents tooth decay; above 1.5 mg/L causes fluorosis.
Mixing up the drinking-water nitrate limit: 45 mg/L as NO₃⁻ (BIS) is about 10 mg/L as N.

questions.q: Classify water pollutants and discuss their effects on human health and the environment.
questions.a:
1. **Oxygen-demanding (biodegradable organic) wastes**: sewage, food, dairy, paper and sugar industry waste. Microbial decomposition consumes DO, raising BOD; fish die, water becomes anaerobic, giving foul smell (H$_2$S).
2. **Pathogens**: bacteria, viruses, protozoa from faeces. Cause cholera, typhoid, dysentery, hepatitis A, polio, diarrhoea.
3. **Plant nutrients** (N, P from fertilisers, detergents): eutrophication, algal blooms, DO depletion, fish kills; nitrate > 45 mg/L causes blue-baby syndrome.
4. **Inorganic chemicals and heavy metals**: Hg (Minamata disease: nerve damage), Cd (itai-itai: painful bone softening, kidney damage), Pb (anaemia, brain damage), As (skin lesions, cancer), F (fluorosis), Cr(VI) (cancer); acids and alkalis kill aquatic life.
5. **Synthetic organic chemicals**: pesticides (DDT, endosulfan), detergents, phenols, PCBs: toxic, carcinogenic, biomagnify; detergents cause foam.
6. **Sediments/suspended solids**: turbidity cuts photosynthesis, clogs gills, silts reservoirs.
7. **Oil**: surface film blocks O$_2$ transfer and light; kills seabirds and marine life.
8. **Radioactive substances**: cancer and genetic mutation.
9. **Thermal pollution**: lowers DO, raises metabolic rates, fish kill.

**Overall effects**: disease and death, loss of aquatic biodiversity, bioaccumulation in food chains, unfit water for agriculture and industry, economic loss.

questions.q: What is eutrophication? Explain its stages and effects.
questions.a:
**Eutrophication** is the nutrient enrichment of a water body (mainly by N and P from fertiliser runoff, sewage and detergents) leading to excessive growth of algae and aquatic plants.

**Stages**: (1) nutrients enter the lake; (2) rapid growth of algae (algal bloom, often blue-green) forms a green scum; (3) the scum blocks sunlight, so submerged plants die; (4) algae die and sink; (5) aerobic bacteria decompose the dead matter and consume DO; (6) DO falls sharply, fish and other organisms die; (7) anaerobic decomposition releases H$_2$S, CH$_4$ and foul smell; the lake gradually fills with organic matter and becomes a marsh.

**Effects**: fish kills, loss of biodiversity, toxins from some blue-green algae, bad taste and odour of drinking water, clogged filters, loss of recreation and fisheries. **Control**: reduce P and N input (phosphate-free detergents, sewage treatment with nutrient removal, controlled fertiliser use), harvesting weeds, aeration.

questions.q: Write short notes on Minamata disease and itai-itai disease.
questions.a:
**Minamata disease**: caused by **methylmercury** in fish and shellfish from Minamata Bay, Japan (1950s), where a chemical factory (Chisso) discharged mercury that bacteria methylated. Symptoms: numbness, loss of vision and hearing, tremors, paralysis, brain damage, birth defects, death.

**Itai-itai ('ouch-ouch') disease**: caused by **cadmium** from zinc mining wastes that contaminated rice fields and drinking water along the Jinzu River, Japan. Symptoms: severe bone and joint pain, softening and fracture of bones (osteomalacia), kidney damage.

questions.q: Why does discharge of untreated sewage into a river cause fish kills?
questions.a: Sewage contains biodegradable organic matter. Aerobic bacteria decompose it and consume dissolved oxygen faster than re-aeration can replace it (high BOD). DO falls below the ~4-5 mg/L that fish need, so fish suffocate. Nutrients in sewage also cause algal blooms that further deplete DO when they decay.

questions.q: Itai-itai disease is caused by:
questions.a: Cadmium causes itai-itai (bone softening and pain). Mercury causes Minamata disease.

questions.q: Eutrophication of a lake is mainly caused by excess of:
questions.a: N and P are the limiting nutrients for algal growth; their excess triggers algal blooms.

questions.q: Skeletal fluorosis is common in areas where drinking water contains fluoride above:
questions.a: BIS (IS 10500) acceptable limit 1.0, permissible 1.5 mg/L; above 1.5 mg/L causes dental and, over time, skeletal fluorosis.

topics.topic: Prevention and control of water pollution
topics.why: Forms the 'control measures' third of the 10-mark water-pollution question; rarely a full question on its own.
topics.gist:
Prevention is cheaper than cure, so answers should move from **source** to **treatment** to **policy**.

**At source (prevention)**
- Waste minimisation and cleaner production in industry: process change, recovery and recycling of water and chemicals, **zero liquid discharge (ZLD)**.
- Separate collection of sewage and storm water; no discharge of untreated sewage.
- Phosphate-free detergents, biodegradable products, eco-friendly idols for immersion.
- In agriculture: balanced fertiliser use, IPM, organic farming, buffer strips, contour farming.
- Safe disposal of solid and hazardous waste so leachate does not reach water; lined landfills.
- Ending open defecation (Swachh Bharat), sanitary toilets.

**Treatment (control)**
- Sewage treatment plants (preliminary, primary, secondary, tertiary) and industrial **effluent treatment plants (ETPs)**; **common effluent treatment plants (CETPs)** for small-industry clusters.
- Specific treatments: neutralisation, chemical precipitation of heavy metals, ion exchange, activated carbon, reverse osmosis.
- Low-cost natural methods: oxidation ponds, constructed wetlands, root-zone treatment, phytoremediation (water hyacinth absorbs metals and nutrients), bioremediation of oil spills.

**Legal and administrative**
- Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974: CPCB and SPCBs, consent to establish and to operate, effluent standards (e.g. BOD ≤ 30 mg/L, COD ≤ 250 mg/L for discharge to inland surface water).
- River action plans: Ganga Action Plan (1985), National River Conservation Plan, **Namami Gange** (2014).
- Monitoring networks, polluter-pays principle, public awareness and participation.

Natural **self-purification** of rivers (dilution, sedimentation, re-aeration, microbial oxidation) helps, but only up to the river's assimilative capacity.
key_points: Prevention at source: cleaner production, recycling, ZLD, separate sewers, phosphate-free detergents.
Agricultural control: fertiliser management, IPM, buffer strips.
Treatment: STPs, ETPs, CETPs; specific chemical treatments.
Low-cost methods: oxidation ponds, constructed wetlands, phytoremediation.
Legal: Water Act 1974, CPCB/SPCB, consent, discharge standards.
Programmes: Ganga Action Plan 1985, Namami Gange 2014.
Self-purification of streams and its limits.

$D_t = \dfrac{k_1 L_0}{k_2 - k_1}\left(e^{-k_1 t} - e^{-k_2 t}\right) + D_0 e^{-k_2 t}$ — Streeter-Phelps oxygen-sag curve (only if covered in class)

Saying the Water Act was passed in 1981. That is the Air Act; the Water Act is 1974.

questions.q: Discuss measures for the prevention and control of water pollution.
questions.a:
**Prevention at source**
1. Cleaner production and waste minimisation in industry; recycle and reuse treated water; zero liquid discharge.
2. Separate sewers for storm water and sewage; no untreated discharge.
3. Phosphate-free detergents, biodegradable chemicals, eco-friendly idols.
4. Balanced use of fertilisers and pesticides; IPM, organic farming; buffer strips along streams.
5. Proper solid-waste disposal; lined landfills; no dumping in rivers.
6. Sanitation: toilets for all, ending open defecation.

**Treatment**
1. Sewage treatment plants (primary, secondary, tertiary).
2. Effluent treatment plants in industries; CETPs for small-scale clusters.
3. Specific methods: neutralisation, precipitation of heavy metals, ion exchange, activated carbon, RO.
4. Low-cost methods: oxidation ponds, constructed wetlands, root-zone treatment, phytoremediation (water hyacinth).

**Legal and administrative**
1. Enforcement of the Water Act 1974 through CPCB and SPCBs: consent to establish/operate, discharge standards, closure of defaulters.
2. Polluter-pays principle; water cess.
3. River cleaning programmes: Ganga Action Plan 1985, Namami Gange 2014.
4. Regular water-quality monitoring.

**Public participation**: awareness campaigns, not throwing waste into water bodies, rainwater harvesting.

questions.q: A river flowing at 10 m³/s has a BOD of 2 mg/L. A town discharges 1 m³/s of wastewater with BOD 200 mg/L into it. Find the BOD just downstream after complete mixing.
questions.a:
$C_{mix} = \dfrac{Q_r C_r + Q_w C_w}{Q_r + Q_w} = \dfrac{10 \times 2 + 1 \times 200}{10 + 1} = \dfrac{220}{11} = 20\ \mathrm{mg/L}$

(This is far above the ~3 mg/L of a clean river, so the wastewater must be treated before discharge.)

questions.q: What is a Common Effluent Treatment Plant (CETP)?
questions.a: A CETP is a centralised effluent treatment facility shared by a cluster of small and medium industries (e.g. tanneries, textile and electroplating units) that cannot afford individual ETPs. Effluents are collected, treated together to the prescribed standards and then discharged, with costs shared among members. It makes treatment affordable and easier for the SPCB to monitor.

questions.q: What is meant by self-purification of a river?
questions.a: Self-purification is the natural recovery of a river's quality downstream of a pollution source through dilution, sedimentation of solids, re-aeration (oxygen from air and photosynthesis), microbial oxidation of organic matter and die-off of pathogens. It works only within the river's assimilative capacity; overloading causes long anaerobic stretches.

questions.q: The Ganga Action Plan was launched in:
questions.a: Ganga Action Plan: 1985. Namami Gange: 2014. Water Act: 1974.

questions.q: Water hyacinth is used in low-cost wastewater treatment because it:
options: Absorbs nutrients and heavy metals from water
questions.a: Phytoremediation: water hyacinth takes up N, P and heavy metals, cleaning the water (it must then be harvested).

topics.why: 'Explain the stages of sewage treatment with a flow diagram' and 'activated sludge process vs trickling filter' are near-certain long questions.
topics.gist:
Sewage is about 99.9% water. The aim of treatment is to remove solids, organic matter (BOD), nutrients and pathogens before discharge or reuse. Learn the **flow sheet**: raw sewage → screens → grit chamber → (skimming tank) → primary clarifier → aeration tank or trickling filter → secondary clarifier → (tertiary/disinfection) → effluent, with a sludge line to digesters and drying beds.

**Preliminary treatment** (physical; protects pumps and later units)
- **Screening**: bar screens (coarse, 25-50 mm; fine, 6-20 mm) remove rags, plastics and floating matter.
- **Grit chamber**: velocity held near 0.3 m/s so heavy inorganic grit (sand, gravel) settles while organic matter stays suspended.
- **Skimming tank** for oil and grease; comminutors shred solids; equalisation tanks for industrial flows.

**Primary treatment** (physical): **plain sedimentation** in primary clarifiers (2-3 h) removes 50-70% of suspended solids and 25-40% of BOD. Chemical coagulation with alum or FeCl$_3$ improves this.

**Secondary (biological) treatment** uses micro-organisms to oxidise dissolved and colloidal organic matter and removes 85-95% of BOD.
- **Activated sludge process (ASP)**: *suspended growth*. Settled sewage is aerated with microbial floc (MLSS 1500-3000 mg/L, 4-8 h). The floc settles in the secondary clarifier, part is returned as **return activated sludge** and the excess is wasted. Compact and efficient, but power-hungry and prone to bulking.
- **Trickling filter**: *attached growth*. Sewage is sprayed by a rotating arm over a bed of stones or plastic media (1-2.5 m deep), and a slime layer (biofilm) oxidises the organics. Simple and low-energy, but needs large area and suffers from flies and odour.
- Others: oxidation ponds, aerated lagoons, rotating biological contactors, UASB reactors.

**Tertiary treatment** removes N and P, polishes by filtration and adsorption, and **disinfects** (chlorine, UV, ozone). **Sludge** is thickened and anaerobically digested (biogas ~60-70% CH$_4$), then dried and used as manure.

Primary: plain sedimentation removes 50-70% SS and 25-40% BOD; optional coagulation.
Secondary: biological oxidation; 85-95% BOD removal.

Trickling filter: rotary distributor, stone media, biofilm, attached growth.
ASP vs trickling filter differences.
Tertiary: nutrient removal, filtration, disinfection; sludge digestion.
formulas: $\text{HRT} = \dfrac{V}{Q}$ — hydraulic retention time
$\dfrac{F}{M} = \dfrac{Q\,S_0}{V\,X}$ — food-to-microorganism ratio ($S_0$ influent BOD, $X$ MLSS)
$\text{SVI (mL/g)} = \dfrac{\text{settled volume after 30 min (mL/L)} \times 1000}{\text{MLSS (mg/L)}}$ — sludge volume index (good settling 50-150)
$\eta = \dfrac{S_0 - S}{S_0} \times 100$ — BOD removal efficiency
$\text{SOR} = \dfrac{Q}{A}$ — surface overflow rate of a clarifier
traps: Saying primary treatment is biological. Primary is physical (sedimentation); secondary is biological.
Putting the grit chamber after the primary clarifier. Screening and grit removal come first.
Calling the trickling filter a filter that strains particles. It is a biological reactor with attached biofilm, not a sieve.
Forgetting the return activated sludge line in the ASP diagram; that recycle is what 'activated' means.
Giving tertiary (disinfection) as secondary treatment.

questions.q: Explain the preliminary, primary and secondary stages of municipal wastewater treatment with a neat flow diagram.
questions.a:
**Flow diagram**: Raw sewage → Bar screens → Grit chamber → Skimming tank → Primary sedimentation tank → Aeration tank (ASP) or Trickling filter → Secondary clarifier → Disinfection (chlorination) → Treated effluent. Sludge from primary and secondary clarifiers → Sludge thickener → Anaerobic digester (biogas) → Sludge drying beds → Manure. Return activated sludge line from secondary clarifier back to the aeration tank.

**1. Preliminary treatment** (physical)
- *Bar screens* remove large floating objects (rags, plastics, wood) that would damage pumps.
- *Grit chamber*: flow velocity kept at about 0.3 m/s so heavy inorganic particles (sand, grit) settle while lighter organics stay in suspension.
- *Skimming tank* removes oil and grease by flotation.

**2. Primary treatment** (physical)
- *Primary sedimentation tank* (detention 2-3 h): suspended organic solids settle as primary sludge. Removes 50-70% of SS and 25-40% of BOD. Coagulants (alum, FeCl$_3$) may be added.

**3. Secondary treatment** (biological)
- *Activated sludge process*: settled sewage is mixed with activated sludge (microbial floc) in an aeration tank and aerated for 4-8 h; microbes oxidise organics: $\text{organics} + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + H_2O + \text{new cells}$. The mixed liquor goes to a secondary clarifier; settled sludge is partly returned to the aeration tank and the excess is wasted.
- *Trickling filter*: settled sewage is sprinkled over a bed of stones (25-75 mm) by a rotary distributor; a biofilm on the stones oxidises organic matter; sloughed biofilm settles in a secondary clarifier.
- Removes 85-95% of BOD and most SS.

**Tertiary/disinfection**: chlorination or UV kills pathogens; optional N and P removal. **Sludge treatment**: thickening, anaerobic digestion producing biogas (60-70% CH$_4$), drying and use as manure.

questions.q: Differentiate between the activated sludge process and the trickling filter.
questions.a:
| Activated sludge process | Trickling filter |
|---|---|
| Suspended-growth process: microbes are suspended as floc | Attached-growth process: microbes grow as biofilm on media |
| Requires mechanical aeration (high power) | Natural ventilation; low power |
| Return of activated sludge is essential | No sludge return (only effluent recirculation in high-rate filters) |
| Compact; less land | Needs more land |
| BOD removal 85-95% | BOD removal 65-90% |
| Sensitive to shock loads, sludge bulking | More robust and simple; problems of flies, odour, ponding |
| Higher operating skill needed | Easy to operate |

questions.q: What is the function of a grit chamber in sewage treatment?
questions.a: A grit chamber removes heavy inorganic particles such as sand, gravel and ash (specific gravity ~2.65) by keeping the flow velocity at about 0.3 m/s, slow enough for grit to settle but fast enough to keep lighter organic matter in suspension. This protects pumps and pipes from abrasion and prevents grit accumulating in later tanks and digesters.

questions.q: In an activated sludge plant, 1 L of mixed liquor settles to 250 mL in 30 minutes and the MLSS is 2500 mg/L. Calculate the SVI and comment.
questions.a:
$\text{SVI} = \dfrac{250 \times 1000}{2500} = 100\ \mathrm{mL/g}$

SVI between about 50 and 150 mL/g indicates good settling sludge; above ~200 indicates bulking.

questions.q: Settled sewage with BOD 250 mg/L leaves the secondary clarifier with BOD 20 mg/L. The aeration tank volume is 1000 m³ and flow is 4000 m³/day. Find the BOD removal efficiency and HRT.
Which of the following is a secondary (biological) treatment unit?
questions.a: The activated sludge process uses microbes to oxidise dissolved organic matter: secondary treatment. The others are preliminary or primary (physical).

questions.q: Primary treatment of sewage mainly removes:
questions.a: Primary sedimentation removes 50-70% of suspended solids (and with them 25-40% of BOD). Dissolved organics need secondary treatment; pathogens and nutrients need tertiary.

questions.q: In a trickling filter, the organic matter is removed by:
options: A microbial biofilm growing on the media
questions.a: It is an attached-growth biological reactor; the slime layer on stones oxidises organics.

topics.why: Definitions and significance of BOD, COD, DO, hardness, TDS and pH, plus BOD/COD/hardness numericals, appear in almost every paper; BOD vs COD is a standard 'differentiate'.
topics.gist:
Each parameter tells you something specific, and the examiner wants **what it is, how it is measured, what it means, and the limit**.

- **pH** (glass-electrode pH meter): drinking water 6.5-8.5 (BIS IS 10500). Acidic water corrodes pipes; alkaline water tastes bitter and scales.
- **TDS** (total dissolved solids): filter, evaporate a known volume, dry at 180 °C (103-105 °C in many class notes) and weigh, or estimate from conductivity. Acceptable 500 mg/L, permissible 2000 mg/L. High TDS gives a salty taste, laxative effect and scaling.
- **Hardness**: due to Ca$^{2+}$ and Mg$^{2+}$. It is determined by **EDTA titration** at pH 10 (NH$_4$Cl-NH$_4$OH buffer) with **Eriochrome Black T**, which changes from wine red to blue. It is expressed as mg/L as CaCO$_3$. Acceptable 200, permissible 600 mg/L. Hard water wastes soap and forms boiler scale.
- **DO** (dissolved oxygen): **Winkler's iodometric method**. MnSO$_4$ and alkaline KI-azide fix the O$_2$ as MnO(OH)$_2$; on acidification it releases I$_2$, which is titrated with thiosulphate using starch indicator. Saturation is about 9 mg/L at 20 °C; fish need more than 4-5 mg/L. Low DO means organic pollution.
- **BOD** (biochemical oxygen demand): oxygen used by **microbes** to oxidise biodegradable organic matter, measured as DO before and after **5 days' incubation at 20 °C** (Indian standards often use 3 days at 27 °C). Clean river < 3 mg/L, raw sewage 200-400 mg/L, discharge limit 30 mg/L.
- **COD** (chemical oxygen demand): oxygen equivalent of organic matter oxidised **chemically** by boiling acidic K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ (Ag$_2$SO$_4$ catalyst, HgSO$_4$ to mask chloride) for 2 h. The excess dichromate is back-titrated with ferrous ammonium sulphate (FAS) using ferroin. It takes about 3 hours. Discharge limit 250 mg/L.

**COD > BOD always**, because dichromate also oxidises non-biodegradable organics. A BOD/COD ratio above about 0.5 means the waste is easily biodegradable; below 0.3 it needs chemical treatment. Bacteriological quality is checked by the coliform MPN test.
key_points: pH: meaning, meter, 6.5-8.5.
TDS: gravimetric method, conductivity estimate; 500/2000 mg/L.
Hardness: temporary vs permanent; EDTA-EBT method at pH 10; as CaCO₃; 200/600 mg/L.
DO: Winkler method reactions; >4-5 mg/L for fish; saturation ~9 mg/L at 20 °C.
BOD: definition, 5-day 20 °C test, formula with dilution, significance.
COD: dichromate reflux, FAS back-titration, formula; COD > BOD.
BOD vs COD differences; BOD/COD ratio and biodegradability.
Typical values and BIS / CPCB limits.
formulas: $\text{BOD (mg/L)} = \dfrac{D_1 - D_2}{P}$ — $D_1, D_2$ initial and final DO of diluted sample, $P$ = volume fraction of sample
$\text{COD (mg/L)} = \dfrac{(A - B) \times N \times 8000}{V_{sample}}$ — $A$ FAS for blank, $B$ FAS for sample (mL), $N$ normality of FAS
$\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 14H^+ + 6e^- \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+} + 7H_2O}$ — dichromate oxidant in COD
$\text{DO (mg/L)} = \dfrac{V_{thio} \times N_{thio} \times 8 \times 1000}{V_{sample}}$ — Winkler
$\mathrm{2Mn(OH)_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2MnO(OH)_2}$;  $\mathrm{MnO(OH)_2 + 4H^+ + 2I^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + I_2 + 3H_2O}$;  $\mathrm{I_2 + 2S_2O_3^{2-} \rightarrow 2I^- + S_4O_6^{2-}}$
$\text{Hardness (mg/L as CaCO}_3) = \dfrac{V_{EDTA} \times M_{EDTA} \times 100 \times 1000}{V_{sample}}$
$\text{CaCO}_3 \text{ equivalent} = \text{mass of salt} \times \dfrac{100}{\text{molar mass of salt}}$ — for a divalent salt (i.e. × 50 / equivalent weight)
$\text{TDS (mg/L)} = \dfrac{(W_2 - W_1)\ (\mathrm{mg}) \times 1000}{V\ (\mathrm{mL})}$;  TDS ≈ 0.55-0.7 × EC (µS/cm)
traps: BOD vs COD: BOD is biological (microbes, 5 days); COD is chemical (dichromate, ~3 h). COD is always ≥ BOD; writing the reverse loses the mark.
Thinking high DO means pollution. LOW DO indicates organic pollution; HIGH BOD indicates pollution.
Expressing hardness in mg/L of Ca²⁺ instead of mg/L as CaCO₃ equivalents.
In the BOD formula, forgetting to divide by the dilution fraction P.
In the COD formula, subtracting the wrong way: it is (blank − sample), because the sample consumes dichromate and leaves less to titrate.
Saying EBT turns from blue to wine red at the endpoint. It is wine red to blue.

questions.q: Define BOD and COD. Differentiate between them and explain why COD is always greater than BOD.
questions.a:
**BOD**: the amount of dissolved oxygen (mg/L) required by aerobic micro-organisms to biochemically oxidise the biodegradable organic matter in a water sample, at 20 °C over 5 days (BOD$_5$).

**COD**: the amount of oxygen (mg/L) equivalent to the organic matter (biodegradable and non-biodegradable) oxidised chemically by a strong oxidant, acidic K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$, under reflux.

| BOD | COD |
|---|---|
| Biological oxidation by microbes | Chemical oxidation by K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ in H$_2$SO$_4$ |
| Measures only biodegradable organics | Measures biodegradable + non-biodegradable organics |
| Takes 5 days (20 °C) | Takes about 3 hours |
| Affected by toxic substances that kill microbes | Not affected by toxicity |
| Lower value | Higher value |

**COD > BOD** because dichromate oxidises almost all organic compounds, including those microbes cannot degrade (lignin, cellulose, some industrial chemicals), and BOD$_5$ captures only part of the ultimate biological demand. The ratio BOD/COD indicates biodegradability (≈0.5 for domestic sewage).

questions.q: In a BOD test, 5 mL of wastewater is diluted to 300 mL. Initial DO is 8.5 mg/L and DO after 5 days at 20 °C is 4.5 mg/L. Calculate the BOD.
questions.a:
$P = \dfrac{5}{300} = 0.01667$

$\text{BOD}_5 = \dfrac{D_1 - D_2}{P} = \dfrac{8.5 - 4.5}{0.01667} = 240\ \mathrm{mg/L}$

(Typical of raw domestic sewage.)

questions.q: In a COD test, 20 mL of sample was refluxed with dichromate. The blank required 20 mL and the sample 12 mL of 0.1 N FAS. Calculate the COD.
questions.a: $\text{COD} = \dfrac{(A - B) \times N \times 8000}{V} = \dfrac{(20 - 12) \times 0.1 \times 8000}{20} = \dfrac{6400}{20} = 320\ \mathrm{mg/L}$

questions.q: 50 mL of a water sample required 12 mL of 0.01 M EDTA for titration using EBT indicator at pH 10. Calculate the total hardness.
questions.a:
Moles of EDTA = moles of (Ca$^{2+}$ + Mg$^{2+}$) = $12 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.01 = 1.2 \times 10^{-4}$ mol, equivalent to $1.2 \times 10^{-4} \times 100 = 0.012$ g = 12 mg CaCO$_3$ in 50 mL.

Hardness $= \dfrac{12 \times 1000}{50} = 240$ mg/L as CaCO$_3$.

(Above the BIS acceptable limit of 200 mg/L but below the permissible 600 mg/L.)

questions.q: Explain the determination of dissolved oxygen by Winkler's method with reactions.
questions.a:
1. To a full BOD bottle of sample add MnSO$_4$ and alkaline KI-azide (azide removes nitrite interference). White Mn(OH)$_2$ forms: $\mathrm{Mn^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Mn(OH)_2}$
2. Dissolved O$_2$ oxidises it to a brown precipitate, fixing the oxygen: $\mathrm{2Mn(OH)_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2MnO(OH)_2}$
3. Add conc. H$_2$SO$_4$; MnO(OH)$_2$ oxidises iodide to iodine: $\mathrm{MnO(OH)_2 + 4H^+ + 2I^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + I_2 + 3H_2O}$
4. Titrate the liberated iodine with standard sodium thiosulphate using starch indicator (blue to colourless): $\mathrm{I_2 + 2S_2O_3^{2-} \rightarrow 2I^- + S_4O_6^{2-}}$

1 mol O$_2$ ≡ 2 mol I$_2$ ≡ 4 mol thiosulphate, so $\text{DO (mg/L)} = \dfrac{V \times N \times 8 \times 1000}{V_{sample}}$.

**Significance**: DO > 5 mg/L supports fish; low DO indicates organic pollution; DO is used in BOD tests and controls aeration in treatment plants.

questions.q: Give the significance of pH and TDS in water quality.
questions.a:
**pH** measures acidity/alkalinity. BIS limit 6.5-8.5. Low pH corrodes pipes and dissolves metals (Pb, Cu); high pH gives bitter taste, scaling and reduces chlorine disinfection efficiency; aquatic life needs a narrow pH range. Measured with a glass-electrode pH meter.

**TDS** is the total inorganic salts and small organics dissolved in water (mg/L), measured by evaporating a filtered sample and weighing the residue, or from conductivity. BIS: 500 acceptable, 2000 permissible. High TDS gives salty taste, laxative effect, scaling in boilers and kettles, and makes water unfit for irrigation.

questions.q: Which statement about BOD and COD is correct?
options: BOD is always greater than COD
COD is always greater than or equal to BOD
BOD and COD are always equal
COD is measured by incubating for 5 days
questions.a: Dichromate oxidises both biodegradable and non-biodegradable organics, so COD ≥ BOD. BOD is the 5-day test.

questions.q: In EDTA titration for hardness using Eriochrome Black T at pH 10, the colour change at the end point is:
questions.a: EBT forms a wine-red complex with Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺; at the end point EDTA takes the metal and free EBT is blue.

topics.why: Asked as 'causes, effects and control of soil pollution' (5-10 marks), usually one of the choices in the end term.
topics.gist:
**Soil pollution** is contamination of soil by substances (chemicals, salts, pathogens, radioactive matter) at levels that harm soil organisms, plants, animals or humans, or reduce soil fertility. Soil degradation is broader and includes erosion; do not mix the two.

**Sources**
- **Agricultural**: excessive chemical fertilisers (acidification, nitrate and cadmium build-up), pesticides and herbicides (persistent organochlorines such as DDT and endosulfan; Kasaragod in Kerala), irrigation with untreated sewage or saline water.
- **Industrial**: heavy metals (Pb, Cd, Cr, Hg, As) from tanneries, electroplating, smelters and battery units; fly ash from thermal plants; dumping of hazardous waste. The Union Carbide site in Bhopal still contaminates soil and groundwater decades after 1984.
- **Urban**: municipal solid waste, plastics, landfill leachate, sewage sludge, e-waste.
- **Mining**: overburden, tailings, acid mine drainage.
- **Others**: acid rain, oil spills, radioactive fallout, biomedical waste.

**Effects**: loss of fertility and soil structure, death of earthworms and microbes, reduced crop yield, toxins taken up into crops and the food chain (biomagnification), contamination of groundwater by leaching, salinity and alkalinity, foul smell and disease from open dumps, and health effects such as cancer and nervous and kidney damage.

**Control**: balanced fertiliser use with soil testing, biofertilisers, compost and organic farming; integrated pest management and biopesticides; proper solid-waste segregation, recycling and sanitary landfills; treatment of industrial waste before disposal; reclamation of mined land. **Remediation**: **bioremediation** (microbes degrade oil and pesticides), **phytoremediation** (Indian mustard *Brassica juncea* for Pb, sunflower for radionuclides), soil washing, liming of acidic soils, gypsum for sodic soils.
key_points: Definition of soil pollution; distinguish from soil erosion.
Sources: agricultural, industrial, urban, mining, others.
Effects on soil, plants, food chain, groundwater and humans.
Control: fertiliser/pesticide management, SWM, industrial waste treatment.
Remediation: bioremediation, phytoremediation, soil washing, liming.
Indian examples: Kasaragod endosulfan; Bhopal UCIL site contamination.
formulas: $\mathrm{CaCO_3 + 2H^+ \rightarrow Ca^{2+} + H_2O + CO_2}$ — liming to neutralise acidic soil
$\mathrm{Na_2\text{-clay} + CaSO_4 \rightarrow Ca\text{-clay} + Na_2SO_4}$ — gypsum reclamation of sodic (alkali) soil
traps: Writing about soil erosion when asked for soil pollution.
Listing sources without effects or control (the question usually wants all three).
Calling phytoremediation 'using pesticides from plants'. It means plants absorb or break down pollutants.
topics.asked_as: 'What is soil pollution? Discuss its causes, effects and control measures' (5-10 marks); 'What is phytoremediation / bioremediation?' (2 marks).

questions.q: Define soil pollution. Discuss its causes, effects and control measures.
questions.a:
**Soil pollution**: the presence of toxic chemicals, salts, pathogens or radioactive substances in soil in concentrations that harm living organisms or reduce soil productivity.

**Causes**
1. Excessive use of chemical fertilisers: soil acidification, nutrient imbalance, nitrate and Cd build-up.
2. Pesticides, insecticides, herbicides: persistent residues (DDT, endosulfan).
3. Industrial wastes: heavy metals from tanneries, electroplating, smelters; fly ash; hazardous chemicals.
4. Urban solid waste and plastics; landfill leachate; sewage sludge.
5. Mining wastes and acid mine drainage.
6. Irrigation with saline water or untreated sewage; waterlogging and salinity.
7. Acid rain, oil spills, radioactive fallout, biomedical and e-waste.

**Effects**
1. Reduced fertility and crop yield; damaged soil structure.
2. Death of beneficial microbes and earthworms.
3. Toxic substances enter food crops and biomagnify.
4. Leaching contaminates groundwater.
5. Health hazards: cancer, kidney, liver and nervous disorders; disease from open dumps.
6. Foul odour and aesthetic damage.

**Control**
1. Need-based fertiliser use; biofertilisers, compost, organic farming.
2. IPM and biopesticides; ban on persistent pesticides.
3. Segregation, recycling and sanitary landfilling of solid waste; reduce plastics.
4. Treatment of industrial wastes before disposal; secure landfills for hazardous waste.
5. Reclamation and afforestation of mined land.
6. Remediation: bioremediation, phytoremediation, soil washing, liming, gypsum.
7. Public awareness and enforcement of waste-management rules.

questions.q: What is phytoremediation? Give two examples.
questions.a: Phytoremediation is the use of green plants to remove, degrade, stabilise or contain pollutants in soil or water. Examples: Indian mustard (*Brassica juncea*) accumulates lead and other heavy metals; sunflower was used to remove radioactive Cs and Sr near Chernobyl; water hyacinth removes metals and nutrients from wastewater.

questions.q: How does excessive use of chemical fertilisers pollute the soil?
questions.a:
1. Ammonium-based fertilisers acidify soil over time.
2. Only NPK is supplied, so micronutrients (Zn, B, Fe) are depleted and organic matter falls.
3. Phosphate fertilisers carry cadmium and fluoride impurities that accumulate.
4. Soil microbes and earthworms decline; soil structure deteriorates.
5. Excess nitrate leaches to groundwater (blue-baby syndrome) and runoff causes eutrophication.

questions.q: Write a short note on bioremediation.
questions.a: Bioremediation is the use of micro-organisms (bacteria, fungi) to degrade or detoxify pollutants in soil or water into harmless products such as CO$_2$ and H$_2$O. It can be *in situ* (treating the site directly, e.g. adding nutrients and oxygen to stimulate native microbes) or *ex situ* (excavated soil treated in biopiles or land farms). Example: oil-eating bacteria (*Pseudomonas*, the 'superbug' developed by Ananda Chakrabarty) for oil spills; TERI's 'Oilzapper' in India. It is cheap and eco-friendly but slow and less effective for heavy metals.

questions.q: Indian mustard (Brassica juncea) is used in phytoremediation of soils contaminated with:
questions.a: It is a hyperaccumulator that takes up Pb, Cd, Cr and other metals into its shoots, which are then harvested.

questions.q: Acidic soils are commonly corrected by adding:
questions.a: Lime neutralises H⁺: CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + H₂O + CO₂. Gypsum is used for sodic (alkaline) soils.

topics.why: Sources, effects and control are a standard 5-10 mark question; the decibel scale, adding noise levels and the Noise Rules 2000 limits give easy numericals and MCQs.
topics.gist:
**Noise** is unwanted or unpleasant sound. **Noise pollution** is noise at a level or duration that harms health, comfort or work. Loudness is measured in **decibels (dB)**, a logarithmic scale relative to the threshold of hearing ($P_0$ = 20 µPa, $I_0$ = 10$^{-12}$ W/m$^2$). An increase of 10 dB means ten times the intensity. Sound-level meters use **A-weighting**, dB(A), to match the ear's sensitivity, and **L$_{eq}$** is the time-averaged level.

Typical levels: whisper 30 dB, conversation 60, busy traffic 80-90, pressure horn and drilling 100, rock concert 110, jet take-off 140. The threshold of pain is ~120-130 dB.

**Sources**: transport (road traffic, horns, rail, aircraft), industry (machines, generators, compressors), construction, loudspeakers, festivals and firecrackers, domestic appliances.

**Effects**
- **Auditory**: temporary threshold shift, then permanent **noise-induced hearing loss** with long exposure (above ~85-90 dB(A) for 8 h), tinnitus, and eardrum rupture at very high levels.
- **Non-auditory**: annoyance, stress, sleep disturbance, high blood pressure and heart disease, headache, interference with speech, lower concentration and efficiency, and effects on wildlife and birds.

**Limits** (Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000, under EPA 1986), in dB(A) L$_{eq}$, day (6 am-10 pm) / night: industrial 75/70, commercial 65/55, residential 55/45, **silence zone 50/40** (100 m around hospitals, educational institutions and courts). Loudspeakers are banned 10 pm-6 am except in permitted cases.

**Control**: at the **source** (silencers, maintenance and lubrication, quieter machines, banning pressure horns), along the **path** (distance, barriers, green belts of dense trees such as neem and ashoka, acoustic insulation and enclosures, double glazing), and at the **receiver** (ear plugs and muffs, job rotation), plus zoning and legal enforcement.
key_points: Definition of noise and noise pollution.
Decibel scale: logarithmic; +10 dB = 10× intensity; +3 dB = doubling of intensity.
dB(A) weighting and Lₑq.
Typical noise levels; threshold of pain ~120-130 dB.
Sources: transport, industry, construction, social and festive.
Auditory and non-auditory effects.
Noise Rules 2000 limits for four zones, day and night; silence zone definition.
Control at source, path and receiver.
formulas: $L_I = 10 \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right),\ I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$ — sound intensity level
$L_p = 20 \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{P}{P_0}\right),\ P_0 = 20\ \mu\mathrm{Pa}$ — sound pressure level
$L_{total} = 10 \log_{10}\left(\sum_i 10^{L_i/10}\right)$ — combining sources (two equal sources: +3 dB)
$L_2 = L_1 - 20 \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}\right)$ — point source in free field (−6 dB per doubling of distance)
traps: Adding decibels arithmetically (80 + 80 = 160 dB). Levels add logarithmically: 80 + 80 = 83 dB.
Mixing up the 10 log (intensity) and 20 log (pressure) formulas.
Wrong zone limits: residential is 55/45, silence 50/40, commercial 65/55, industrial 75/70 dB(A).

Saying the Noise Rules are under the Air Act. They were framed under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986. (Noise was added to the Air Act's definition of air pollutant in 1987, which is a separate fact.)
Listing only hearing loss as an effect. Non-auditory effects are half the marks.
topics.asked_as: 'Define noise pollution. Discuss its sources, effects and control measures' (10 marks); 'What is a decibel?' (2 marks); numericals on adding levels or converting intensity (2-3 marks); MCQs on permissible limits.

questions.q: What is noise pollution? Describe its sources, effects and control measures.
questions.a:
**Noise pollution**: unwanted sound of high intensity or long duration that causes discomfort, damages health or reduces efficiency. Measured in dB(A).

**Sources**
1. Transport: road traffic, horns, motorbikes, trains, aircraft.
2. Industrial: machines, generators, compressors, presses, mills.
3. Construction: drilling, pile driving, concrete mixers.
4. Social/festive: loudspeakers, DJ systems, firecrackers, processions.
5. Domestic: TV, music systems, mixers, coolers.

**Effects**
*Auditory*: temporary threshold shift; permanent noise-induced hearing loss on long exposure above ~90 dB(A); tinnitus; eardrum rupture above ~150 dB.
*Non-auditory*: annoyance, irritability, stress; sleep disturbance; hypertension, heart disease; headache, fatigue; interference with speech and learning; reduced work efficiency and accidents; effects on animals (stress, migration of birds).

**Control**
1. *At source*: silencers and mufflers, proper maintenance and lubrication, quieter machine design, vibration dampers, banning pressure horns.
2. *Along the path*: increasing distance, noise barriers, green belts of dense trees (neem, ashoka, tamarind), acoustic enclosures, sound-absorbing materials, double-glazed windows.
3. *At the receiver*: ear plugs and ear muffs, limiting exposure time, job rotation.
4. *Legal and planning*: Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000 limits; silence zones around hospitals and schools; ban on loudspeakers 10 pm-6 am; land-use zoning that keeps industries and airports away from homes; public awareness.

questions.q: Three machines produce noise levels of 85 dB, 88 dB and 90 dB at a point. Find the combined noise level.
Find the sound intensity level for an intensity of 10⁻⁵ W/m², and the sound pressure level for a pressure of 2 Pa.
State the ambient noise standards in India for different zones.
questions.a:
Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000, limits in dB(A) L$_{eq}$:

| Zone | Day (6 am-10 pm) | Night (10 pm-6 am) |
|---|---|---|
| Industrial | 75 | 70 |
| Commercial | 65 | 55 |
| Residential | 55 | 45 |
| Silence zone | 50 | 40 |

A silence zone is an area within 100 m of hospitals, educational institutions and courts.

questions.q: Two identical machines each produce 80 dB. When both run together the noise level is:
questions.a: $10\log_{10}(2 \times 10^8) = 80 + 10\log_{10}2 = 83$ dB. Doubling intensity adds 3 dB.

questions.q: The permissible daytime noise limit in a residential area in India is:
questions.a: Residential: 55 dB(A) day, 45 dB(A) night.

questions.q: A noise source gives 90 dB at 10 m. Estimate the level at 40 m (free-field point source).
questions.a: $L_2 = L_1 - 20\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{40}{10}\right) = 90 - 20 \times 0.602 = 90 - 12 = 78\ \mathrm{dB}$ (−6 dB for each doubling of distance, twice).

topics.why: Usually one 5-mark 'sources, effects and control' question or a short note on cooling towers; the DO-temperature link is the idea the examiner checks.
topics.gist:
**Thermal pollution** is the degradation of water quality by any process that changes the ambient water temperature, usually by discharging **heated water** into rivers, lakes or the sea.

**Sources**
- **Thermal power plants**: coal plants convert only ~35% of fuel energy to electricity, and most of the rest is rejected as heat in condenser cooling water. In a once-through system that water is returned to the river 8-10 °C warmer.
- **Nuclear power plants**: even more waste heat per unit of electricity.
- Industries: steel, refineries, paper, textiles, chemicals.
- Hot urban runoff from roads and roofs, domestic sewage, removal of shade trees along banks.
- Cold-water releases from the bottom of deep reservoirs, which are also a form of thermal pollution.

**Effects**
1. **Less dissolved oxygen**: O$_2$ solubility falls with temperature (~14.6 mg/L at 0 °C, ~9.1 at 20 °C, ~7.6 at 30 °C).
2. At the same time warmer water **raises the metabolic rate** and oxygen demand of fish and the rate of microbial decomposition, so oxygen stress is doubled.
3. **Thermal shock** and fish kills when temperature changes suddenly (start-up or shutdown of a plant).
4. Disruption of **spawning, migration** and egg hatching; loss of sensitive species and biodiversity.
5. Higher **toxicity** of pollutants and faster multiplication of pathogens.
6. Favours **blue-green algal** blooms over useful algae.

**Control**: **cooling towers** (wet evaporative, natural-draft hyperbolic or mechanical-draft; dry towers in water-scarce areas), **cooling ponds** and **spray ponds**, artificial lakes, recirculating instead of once-through cooling, and reuse of waste heat (cogeneration, district heating, greenhouses, aquaculture). CPCB norms limit the discharge to no more than **5 °C above** the intake water temperature.
key_points: Definition of thermal pollution.
Sources: thermal and nuclear power plants (main), industries, urban runoff, deforestation of banks.
DO solubility decreases with temperature (Henry's law constant changes).
Effects: DO depletion + higher metabolic demand, thermal shock, spawning disruption, toxicity, algal blooms.
Control: cooling towers (wet/dry; natural/mechanical draft), cooling ponds, spray ponds, artificial lakes, waste-heat recovery.
Standard: discharge ≤ 5 °C above intake water temperature.
formulas: $Q = \dot m\, c_p\, \Delta T$ — heat carried away by cooling water ($c_p$ = 4186 J/kg K)
$C = k_H \cdot p_{O_2}$ — Henry's law; $k_H$ for O₂ decreases as temperature rises
traps: Saying warm water holds more oxygen. It holds LESS.
Forgetting the double effect: less oxygen available AND more oxygen demanded.
Thinking a cooling tower 'cleans' the water. It removes heat; the water is then recirculated.
Calling hot air from chimneys 'thermal pollution' in the syllabus sense. The topic is about water bodies.
topics.asked_as: 'What is thermal pollution? Discuss its sources, effects and control' (5-10 marks); 'Explain the working of cooling towers/ponds' (3-5 marks); 'Why does thermal pollution reduce DO?' (2 marks).

questions.q: Define thermal pollution. Describe its sources, effects and control methods.
questions.a:
**Thermal pollution**: the degradation of water quality caused by a change (usually an increase) in the ambient temperature of a water body due to human activity.

**Sources**: (i) thermal power plants (main source; condenser cooling water); (ii) nuclear power plants; (iii) industries such as steel, refineries, paper, textiles; (iv) domestic sewage and hot urban runoff; (v) deforestation of river banks; (vi) cold water releases from deep reservoirs.

**Effects**
1. Reduced DO, since gas solubility falls with temperature.
2. Increased metabolic rate and O$_2$ demand of aquatic organisms; faster decomposition raises BOD.
3. Thermal shock and fish kills due to sudden temperature changes.
4. Disturbance of reproduction, spawning, migration; eggs fail to hatch.
5. Increased toxicity of chemicals (e.g. cyanide, heavy metals) and growth of pathogens.
6. Replacement of useful algae by blue-green algae; loss of biodiversity.

**Control**
1. **Cooling towers**: hot water is sprayed/trickled down while air flows upward; heat is lost mainly by evaporation (wet towers) or through finned tubes (dry towers); natural-draft (hyperbolic) or mechanical-draft (fans). The cooled water is recirculated.
2. **Cooling ponds**: large shallow ponds where hot water loses heat by evaporation, convection and radiation.
3. **Spray ponds**: water is sprayed through nozzles into the air as fine droplets for faster cooling.
4. **Artificial lakes** used as heat sinks.
5. **Reuse of waste heat**: cogeneration, district heating, greenhouses, aquaculture.
6. Enforcing standards: discharge not more than 5 °C above intake temperature.

questions.q: A power plant passes 10 m³/s of cooling water through its condenser and the water temperature rises by 8 °C. Calculate the rate of heat rejected to the river.
questions.a:
$\dot m = 10\ \mathrm{m^3/s} \times 1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} = 10^4\ \mathrm{kg/s}$

$Q = \dot m\, c_p\, \Delta T = 10^4 \times 4186 \times 8 = 3.35 \times 10^8\ \mathrm{W} \approx 335\ \mathrm{MW}$

questions.q: Explain why thermal pollution is harmful to fish even though the temperature rise is only a few degrees.
questions.a: Warmer water dissolves less oxygen (e.g. ~9.1 mg/L at 20 °C vs ~7.6 at 30 °C). At the same time fish are cold-blooded, so their metabolic rate and oxygen requirement increase with temperature (roughly doubling for every 10 °C), and bacterial decomposition also speeds up. So oxygen supply falls while demand rises. Sudden changes cause thermal shock, and many species have narrow temperature ranges for spawning and egg development.

questions.q: What is a cooling pond? How does it differ from a spray pond?
questions.a: A **cooling pond** is a large, shallow man-made pond into which hot water is discharged; it cools by evaporation, convection and radiation from the surface before reuse or discharge. It needs a large area. A **spray pond** sprays the hot water into the air through nozzles as fine droplets, which greatly increases the surface area and cools the water faster in a smaller area, but with more evaporative water loss.

questions.q: The main source of thermal pollution of water bodies is:
options: Cooling water from thermal and nuclear power plants
questions.a: Condenser cooling water discharged from power plants is the largest source of heated effluent.

questions.q: With an increase in water temperature, the solubility of oxygen in water:
questions.a: Gas solubility decreases with temperature, which is the central harm of thermal pollution.

topics.why: Sources, effects and control appear as a 5-10 mark option; units (Bq, Gy, Sv), half-life and the Chernobyl/Fukushima examples give short questions.
topics.gist:
**Radioactive (nuclear) pollution** is the increase in natural background radiation caused by human activities that release radioactive substances or radiation into the environment.

**Radiation types**: **α** particles (He nuclei) are stopped by paper but are very damaging inside the body. **β** particles (electrons) are stopped by a few mm of aluminium. **γ** rays and X-rays are penetrating and need lead or concrete. All are **ionising**: they break bonds and damage DNA.

**Sources**
- **Natural**: cosmic rays, radon gas from soil and rock (the largest natural dose), K-40, U and Th in rocks.
- **Anthropogenic**: nuclear weapon tests (fallout), nuclear reactors and accidents (**Chernobyl 1986, Fukushima 2011**), uranium mining and fuel processing, radioactive waste, medical X-rays, CT and radiotherapy, industrial radiography and research isotopes.

**Important isotopes**: **I-131** (half-life 8 days) concentrates in the thyroid, causing thyroid cancer. **Sr-90** (~29 years) behaves like Ca and lodges in bone (bone cancer, leukaemia). **Cs-137** (~30 years) behaves like K and spreads through muscle.

**Effects**: *somatic* (on the exposed person): radiation burns, sickness, hair loss, cataract, leukaemia and cancers, and death at high doses. *Genetic*: mutations passed to offspring. Ecosystems are affected through bioaccumulation.

**Units**: activity in becquerel (1 decay/s; 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10$^{10}$ Bq). Absorbed dose in gray (1 J/kg; 1 rad = 0.01 Gy). Equivalent dose in sievert ($H = D \times w_R$, with $w_R$ = 20 for α and 1 for β and γ; 1 rem = 0.01 Sv). The public dose limit is 1 mSv/year.

**Control**: safe reactor design and siting, containment and monitoring, regulation by AERB (India), safe disposal of waste (low-level waste diluted or buried; high-level waste vitrified and stored in deep geological repositories), the ALARA principle, shielding, time and distance protection, and minimising unnecessary medical X-rays.

Natural vs anthropogenic sources; radon as largest natural dose.
Key isotopes: I-131 (thyroid), Sr-90 (bone), Cs-137 (muscle).
Somatic and genetic effects.
Units: Bq, Ci, Gy, rad, Sv, rem; dose limits.
Half-life and decay law.
Nuclear accidents: Chernobyl 1986, Fukushima 2011.
Control and nuclear waste disposal (LLW, HLW vitrification, geological repository).
formulas: $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ — radioactive decay law
$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$ — half-life
$N = N_0 \left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/t_{1/2}}$ — fraction remaining after $t$
$A = \lambda N$ — activity (Bq); $1\ \mathrm{Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{Bq}$
$H\ (\mathrm{Sv}) = D\ (\mathrm{Gy}) \times w_R$ — equivalent dose ($w_R$: α 20, β and γ 1)
traps: Saying α particles are harmless because they are stopped by paper. They are the most damaging when inhaled or ingested.
Mixing gray (absorbed energy) and sievert (biological effect).
Matching the isotope to the wrong organ: I-131 thyroid, Sr-90 bone, Cs-137 muscle/soft tissue.
Saying that after two half-lives the substance is gone. One quarter remains.
