questions.q: What is radioactive pollution? Discuss its sources, effects and control measures.
questions.a:
**Radioactive pollution**: the increase above natural background levels of ionising radiation in the environment due to the release of radioactive substances by human activities.

**Sources**
*Natural*: cosmic rays; radon-222 from soil and building materials; K-40, U-238, Th-232 in rocks and soil.
*Man-made*: (i) nuclear weapon tests (fallout of Sr-90, Cs-137, I-131); (ii) nuclear power plants: routine releases and accidents (Chernobyl 1986, Fukushima 2011); (iii) mining and processing of uranium; (iv) nuclear fuel reprocessing and radioactive waste; (v) medical uses: X-rays, CT, radiotherapy, radioisotopes; (vi) industrial and research uses of isotopes.

**Effects**
*Somatic* (on the exposed individual): skin burns, radiation sickness (nausea, vomiting, hair loss), cataract, sterility, leukaemia and cancers of thyroid, bone and lungs, shortened life span, death at high doses.
*Genetic*: mutations in reproductive cells passed to future generations; birth defects.
*Specific isotopes*: I-131 accumulates in the thyroid; Sr-90 replaces Ca in bones; Cs-137 spreads in muscles.
*Environmental*: contamination of soil, water and food chains; bioaccumulation.

**Control**
1. Safe design, siting and operation of reactors; containment; emergency plans.
2. Regulation and monitoring (AERB in India); dose limits (public 1 mSv/yr).
3. Proper waste management: LLW diluted or buried in shallow trenches; HLW vitrified in glass, sealed in steel canisters and stored in deep geological repositories.
4. Shielding (lead, concrete), minimum time and maximum distance for workers; ALARA principle.
5. Avoid unnecessary medical X-rays; radon ventilation in buildings.
6. Ban on nuclear tests (CTBT).

questions.q: I-131 has a half-life of 8 days. What fraction of an initial sample remains after 24 days?
questions.a: $\dfrac{N}{N_0} = \left(\tfrac12\right)^{24/8} = \left(\tfrac12\right)^3 = \tfrac18 = 12.5\%$

questions.q: Differentiate between gray and sievert.
questions.a: **Gray (Gy)** is the unit of absorbed dose: 1 Gy = 1 joule of radiation energy absorbed per kg of matter (old unit rad = 0.01 Gy). **Sievert (Sv)** is the unit of equivalent (biological) dose, which accounts for the type of radiation: $H = D \times w_R$ ($w_R$ = 20 for α, 1 for β and γ). Old unit rem = 0.01 Sv.

questions.q: How is high-level nuclear waste disposed of?
questions.a: High-level waste (spent fuel, reprocessing residues) is highly radioactive and generates heat. Steps: (i) cooling for several years in water pools at the reactor; (ii) **vitrification**: the waste is mixed with borosilicate glass and solidified; (iii) sealed in stainless steel canisters; (iv) interim storage in shielded, cooled facilities; (v) final disposal in **deep geological repositories** (stable rock formations several hundred metres underground) with multiple engineered barriers (canister, bentonite clay, rock). It must be isolated for thousands of years.

questions.q: Strontium-90 is dangerous because it accumulates in:
questions.a: Sr is chemically similar to Ca, so Sr-90 is deposited in bones, causing bone cancer and leukaemia. I-131 targets the thyroid.

questions.q: The SI unit of radioactivity (activity) is:
questions.a: 1 becquerel = 1 disintegration per second. Gray is absorbed dose; sievert is equivalent dose.

topics.why: 'Types, sources and methods of disposal of solid waste' and the waste-management hierarchy are frequent 10-mark questions; composting, landfill and incineration are common short notes.
topics.gist:
**Solid waste** is any discarded solid or semi-solid material from domestic, commercial, industrial, agricultural or other activities. Main types: **municipal solid waste (MSW)**, industrial waste (fly ash, slag), **hazardous waste** (toxic, flammable, corrosive, reactive), **biomedical waste**, **e-waste**, construction and demolition waste, and agricultural waste. India generates about 1.5-1.7 lakh tonnes of MSW per day. Roughly half of it is wet, biodegradable organic matter, the rest paper, plastic, glass, metal and inerts.

**Functional elements of SWM**: generation → storage and **segregation at source** → collection → transfer and transport → processing and recovery → disposal.

**Waste-management hierarchy** (most to least preferred, an inverted pyramid): **Prevention/Reduce → Reuse → Recycle → Recover (energy) → Dispose (landfill)**.

**Methods**
- **Composting**: aerobic decomposition of organic waste into humus-like manure at 55-65 °C, which kills pathogens. The optimum C/N ratio is ~25-30. Variants are windrow composting and **vermicomposting** with earthworms.
- **Anaerobic digestion / biomethanation**: gives biogas and slurry.
- **Incineration**: controlled burning at ≥850 °C reduces volume by ~90% and can generate energy, but emits dioxins, furans and fly ash and needs high-calorific, dry waste.
- **Pyrolysis and gasification**: heating with no or limited oxygen gives fuel gas, oil and char.
- **Sanitary landfill**: an engineered site with a clay or HDPE **liner**, leachate collection and treatment, daily soil cover, gas venting or methane recovery, and a final cap. It is different from an **open dump**, which causes leachate, fires, methane and disease.
- **Recycling**: paper, plastics, metals, glass; refuse-derived fuel (RDF).

**Rules** (all 2016, under EPA 1986): Solid Waste Management Rules (three-way segregation into wet, dry and domestic hazardous), Plastic Waste Management Rules, E-Waste Rules (revised 2022), Bio-Medical Waste Rules (colour-coded bags: yellow, red, white and blue), Hazardous Waste Rules. Swachh Bharat Mission dates from 2014. **Indore**, MP, has been ranked India's cleanest city for several years running thanks to strict segregation and processing.
key_points: Definition and classification of solid waste (MSW, industrial, hazardous, biomedical, e-waste, C&D, agricultural).
Composition of Indian MSW (~50% organic).
Functional elements: generation, segregation/storage, collection, transfer/transport, processing, disposal.
Hierarchy: reduce > reuse > recycle > recover > dispose.
Composting (aerobic; C/N 25-30) and vermicomposting; biomethanation.
Incineration: merits and demerits (dioxins).
Sanitary landfill vs open dumping; liner, leachate, gas collection, cover.
SWM Rules 2016 and related rules; biomedical waste colour coding.
formulas: $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O + heat}$ — aerobic composting
$\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 \rightarrow 3CH_4 + 3CO_2}$ — anaerobic decomposition in landfills/digesters
$V = \dfrac{M}{\rho_{compacted}}$ — landfill volume needed for a waste mass $M$
traps: Treating a sanitary landfill as the best option. It is the LAST step in the hierarchy.
Calling an open dump a landfill. A sanitary landfill must have a liner, leachate collection, daily cover and gas control.
Saying composting is anaerobic. Composting is aerobic; anaerobic digestion gives biogas.
Recommending incineration for wet Indian MSW without noting its low calorific value and dioxin emissions.
Getting the hierarchy order wrong (recycle before reuse).

questions.q: What is solid waste management? Discuss the various methods of solid waste disposal with their merits and demerits.
questions.a:
**Solid waste management** is the systematic control of generation, storage, segregation, collection, transport, processing, recovery and disposal of solid waste in a way that protects public health and the environment and is economical.

**Methods**
1. **Sanitary landfill**: waste is spread in thin layers, compacted and covered daily with soil in an engineered site with an impermeable liner, leachate collection and gas venting. *Merits*: simple, handles all waste, methane recovery. *Demerits*: large land area, leachate and methane risk, last resort.
2. **Composting**: aerobic microbial decomposition of segregated organic waste in windrows or pits into manure (thermophilic phase 55-65 °C kills pathogens). *Merits*: returns nutrients to soil, reduces waste volume, low cost. *Demerits*: needs segregation, odour and flies if poorly managed, time (6-8 weeks). *Vermicomposting* uses earthworms.
3. **Incineration**: controlled combustion at ≥850 °C. *Merits*: 80-90% volume reduction, energy recovery, destroys pathogens (biomedical waste). *Demerits*: high cost, dioxins, furans, heavy metals in ash; Indian wet waste has low calorific value.
4. **Pyrolysis/gasification**: thermal decomposition without/with limited oxygen into gas, oil and char. *Merits*: fuel recovery, fewer emissions. *Demerits*: expensive, needs dry sorted waste.
5. **Anaerobic digestion (biomethanation)**: organic waste digested to biogas and slurry. *Merits*: energy and manure. *Demerits*: needs segregated wet waste and process control.
6. **Recycling and reuse**: paper, plastics, glass, metals recovered. *Merits*: saves resources and energy. *Demerits*: needs segregation; informal sector health risks.
7. **Open dumping** (to be avoided): cheap but causes leachate, fires, methane, flies, rodents and disease.

Preferred order follows the hierarchy: reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose.

questions.q: Explain the solid waste management hierarchy.
questions.a:
The hierarchy ranks options from most to least preferred (drawn as an inverted pyramid):
1. **Prevention / Reduce**: avoid generating waste (less packaging, durable products, buy only what is needed). Most preferred.
2. **Reuse**: use items again for the same or another purpose (refill bottles, cloth bags, repair).
3. **Recycle**: reprocess materials into new products (paper, metals, glass, plastic); composting of organics.
4. **Recover**: recover energy from residual waste (incineration with energy recovery, RDF, biogas).
5. **Dispose**: safe disposal of what remains in a sanitary landfill. Least preferred.

Moving up the hierarchy saves resources and energy and reduces pollution.

questions.q: List the essential features of a sanitary landfill.
questions.a:
1. Site away from habitation and water sources, on low-permeability ground.
2. Bottom liner of compacted clay and HDPE geomembrane.
3. Leachate collection pipes and treatment.
4. Waste spread in thin layers, compacted, and covered daily with 15-20 cm soil.
5. Gas venting or collection of methane for energy.
6. Final cover (cap) with clay, soil and vegetation.
7. Monitoring wells for groundwater and gas.

questions.q: A city generates 500 tonnes of MSW per day. If the waste is compacted to 800 kg/m³ in a landfill, what volume is needed per day and per year?
questions.a:
$V_{day} = \dfrac{500 \times 1000\ \mathrm{kg}}{800\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}} = 625\ \mathrm{m^3/day}$

$V_{year} = 625 \times 365 \approx 2.28 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{m^3}$ (excluding cover soil). This shows why reducing and composting waste is essential.

questions.q: In the solid waste management hierarchy, the most preferred option is:
questions.a: Prevention/reduction tops the hierarchy; landfill is the last resort.

questions.q: Composting of municipal solid waste is essentially a process of:
questions.a: Composting is aerobic microbial decomposition into humus-like manure; anaerobic digestion is a different process that produces biogas.

questions.q: What is e-waste? Why is it hazardous?
questions.a: E-waste is discarded electrical and electronic equipment: computers, phones, TVs, batteries, refrigerators, etc. It is hazardous because it contains lead (solder, CRTs), mercury (switches, lamps), cadmium (batteries), chromium(VI), brominated flame retardants and PVC. Crude informal recycling (open burning, acid baths) releases dioxins and heavy metals into air, soil and water, harming workers and nearby communities. It is regulated by the E-Waste (Management) Rules (2016, revised 2022) under extended producer responsibility.

topics.why: Definition, the GHGs and their GWP, the scopes and reduction strategies are frequent 2-5 mark questions, and a simple household footprint calculation is an easy numerical.
topics.gist:
A **carbon footprint** is the total amount of greenhouse gases emitted, directly and indirectly, by an individual, organisation, event, product or country, expressed as **CO$_2$-equivalent (CO$_2$e)**, usually in tonnes per year.

Different gases are converted to CO$_2$e with their **global warming potential (GWP)** over 100 years: CO$_2$ = 1, CH$_4$ ≈ 28 (IPCC AR5; older notes use 21 or 25), N$_2$O ≈ 265 (older notes 298 or 310), SF$_6$ ≈ 23,500, and HFCs in the hundreds to thousands.

**Calculation**: footprint = Σ (activity data × emission factor). Rough emission factors: grid electricity in India ~0.7-0.8 kg CO$_2$/kWh (coal-heavy), petrol ~2.3 kg CO$_2$/litre, diesel ~2.7 kg/L, LPG ~3 kg/kg. Burning 1 kg of carbon gives 44/12 = 3.67 kg CO$_2$.

**Scopes** (GHG Protocol) for organisations:
- **Scope 1**: direct emissions from owned sources (boilers, vehicles, DG sets).
- **Scope 2**: indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heat or steam.
- **Scope 3**: all other value-chain emissions (purchased goods, travel, commuting, waste, use of sold products). Usually the largest.

India's per-capita emission is ~2 t CO$_2$/year, against a world average of ~4.7 and the USA at ~14. India's total is the third largest. India has pledged **net zero by 2070** (COP26 'Panchamrit').

**Reducing the footprint**: energy efficiency (LEDs, star-rated appliances), renewable electricity (rooftop solar), public transport, cycling and electric vehicles, less meat and food waste, the 3Rs, fewer flights, afforestation. **Offsetting** means buying **carbon credits** (1 credit = 1 tonne CO$_2$e avoided or removed, from the Kyoto CDM, voluntary markets, or India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme 2023). Related ideas are the water footprint and the ecological footprint.
key_points: Definition: total direct + indirect GHG emissions in CO₂e.
Greenhouse gases and their GWPs (state the source/IPCC report you use).
Calculation: activity × emission factor; CO₂e = mass × GWP.
Scope 1, 2, 3 emissions.
Typical values: India ~2 t/person/yr, world ~4.7.
Reduction strategies at individual, institutional and national levels.
Carbon credits and offsetting; India's net-zero 2070 target.
formulas: $CF = \sum_i A_i \times EF_i$ — footprint = Σ activity data × emission factor
$\mathrm{CO_2e} = \sum_j m_j \times GWP_j$ — conversion of other GHGs
$\mathrm{C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$: 1 kg C → $\tfrac{44}{12} = 3.67$ kg CO₂
$\mathrm{C_8H_{18} + 12.5\,O_2 \rightarrow 8CO_2 + 9H_2O}$ — petrol (as octane) combustion, ~3.09 kg CO₂ per kg fuel
traps: Counting only CO₂. The footprint includes CH₄, N₂O and F-gases as CO₂e.
Quoting GWP values without naming the source. Textbooks differ (CH₄ 21 in SAR, 25 in AR4, 28 in AR5, ~27-30 in AR6); state which you use.
Confusing carbon footprint with ecological footprint (land area in global hectares).
Mixing kg of carbon and kg of CO₂ (factor 3.67).
Putting purchased electricity in Scope 1. It is Scope 2.
topics.asked_as: 'What is carbon footprint? How can it be reduced?' (5 marks); 'Define carbon footprint and GWP' (2 marks); a household/hostel footprint calculation (3 marks); 'Explain Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions' (3 marks).

questions.q: Define carbon footprint. Explain how it is calculated and suggest measures to reduce it.
questions.a:
**Carbon footprint**: the total greenhouse gas emissions caused directly and indirectly by an individual, organisation, event, product or nation, expressed in tonnes of CO$_2$-equivalent per year.

**Calculation**
1. List all emission-causing activities (electricity, fuels, transport, food, goods, waste).
2. Collect activity data (kWh, litres, km, kg).
3. Multiply by emission factors (e.g. ~0.8 kg CO$_2$/kWh grid electricity, ~2.3 kg CO$_2$/L petrol).
4. Convert non-CO$_2$ gases using GWP: CO$_2$e = mass × GWP (CH$_4$ ≈ 28, N$_2$O ≈ 265).
5. Sum: $CF = \sum A_i \times EF_i$. For organisations, report as Scope 1 (direct), Scope 2 (purchased energy), Scope 3 (value chain).

**Reduction measures**
- *Energy*: LED lighting, star-rated appliances, switching off devices, rooftop solar, green buildings.
- *Transport*: public transport, cycling, walking, car-pooling, EVs, fewer flights.
- *Food*: more plant-based diet, local seasonal food, less food waste.
- *Waste*: reduce, reuse, recycle, compost; avoid single-use plastic.
- *Institutional*: energy audits, renewable power purchase, efficient processes, afforestation.
- *Offsetting*: carbon credits from verified projects.

questions.q: A household uses 250 kWh of electricity per month (emission factor 0.8 kg CO₂/kWh), 40 litres of petrol per month (2.3 kg CO₂/L), and one 14.2 kg LPG cylinder per month (3.0 kg CO₂/kg). Calculate its annual carbon footprint from these sources.
questions.a:
Monthly:
- Electricity: $250 \times 0.8 = 200$ kg CO$_2$
- Petrol: $40 \times 2.3 = 92$ kg CO$_2$
- LPG: $14.2 \times 3.0 = 42.6$ kg CO$_2$

Total per month $= 334.6$ kg CO$_2$

Annual $= 334.6 \times 12 = 4015$ kg $\approx 4.0$ t CO$_2$ per year.

Electricity is the largest share (~60%), so efficiency and rooftop solar would reduce the footprint most.

questions.q: A landfill releases 10 tonnes of methane per year. Express this as CO₂-equivalent (take GWP of CH₄ = 28).
questions.a: $\mathrm{CO_2e} = 10 \times 28 = 280$ tonnes CO$_2$e per year. (With older values GWP = 25 it would be 250 t; state the value used.)

questions.q: Explain Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions with examples for a university campus.
questions.a:
**Scope 1** (direct): emissions from sources owned or controlled by the campus, e.g. diesel generators, campus buses, LPG in hostel messes, refrigerant leaks.
**Scope 2** (indirect, energy): emissions from generating the electricity, steam or heat the campus purchases, e.g. grid electricity for labs and hostels.
**Scope 3** (other indirect): all other value-chain emissions, e.g. students' and staff commuting, air travel for conferences, purchased food, paper and equipment, waste disposal, construction materials.

questions.q: Carbon footprint is generally expressed in terms of:
questions.a: All GHGs are converted to CO₂-equivalent using GWP. Land area is the ecological footprint.

questions.q: Emissions from electricity purchased from the grid are classified as:
questions.a: Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heat or steam.

topics.why: 'What is LCA? Explain its stages/phases' is a common 5-10 mark question; examiners check the four ISO phases and the cradle-to-grave life stages.
topics.gist:
**Life cycle assessment (LCA)** is a method for evaluating the environmental impacts of a product, process or service over its **entire life cycle**, from raw-material extraction to final disposal ('cradle to grave'). It is standardised in **ISO 14040 and ISO 14044**.

**Life-cycle stages** (what is studied):
1. raw-material acquisition (mining, farming, extraction);
2. material processing and manufacturing;
3. packaging, transportation and distribution;
4. use, operation and maintenance;
5. end of life: reuse, recycling, incineration or landfill.

**Four phases of an LCA study** (how it is done, ISO 14040):
1. **Goal and scope definition**: purpose, intended audience, the **functional unit** (e.g. 'packaging 1000 L of milk' or 'lighting 1 m² for 10 years'), system boundaries, assumptions.
2. **Life cycle inventory (LCI)**: quantify all inputs (energy, water, materials) and outputs (emissions to air, water and soil, waste) for every stage.
3. **Life cycle impact assessment (LCIA)**: assign inventory flows to impact categories (*classification*) and quantify them (*characterisation*): global warming (kg CO$_2$e), acidification (kg SO$_2$e), eutrophication, ozone depletion, smog formation, human toxicity, resource depletion, water use. Normalisation and weighting are optional.
4. **Interpretation**: identify hotspots, check sensitivity and uncertainty, draw conclusions and recommendations. It is iterative with the other phases.

**Boundaries**: cradle-to-grave, cradle-to-gate (up to the factory gate), gate-to-gate, and **cradle-to-cradle** (closed loop, with materials recycled into new products).

**Uses**: comparing products (paper vs plastic vs cloth bags), eco-design, eco-labelling (India's Ecomark), avoiding burden-shifting, and supporting policy and green procurement. **Limitations**: data-intensive and costly, results depend on assumptions and boundaries, and local impacts are hard to capture.
key_points: Definition: cradle-to-grave environmental assessment; ISO 14040/14044.
Five life-cycle stages of a product.
Four phases: goal & scope, inventory (LCI), impact assessment (LCIA), interpretation.
Functional unit and system boundary: meaning and examples.
Impact categories and their units.
Cradle-to-grave, cradle-to-gate, gate-to-gate, cradle-to-cradle.
Applications and limitations; an example comparison.
formulas: $\text{Impact}_k = \sum_i m_i \times CF_{i,k}$ — characterisation: inventory mass × characterisation factor for category $k$ (e.g. GWP for climate change)
$\text{Total} = \sum_{\text{stages}} \text{impact}_{stage}$ — summing over raw material, manufacture, transport, use, end of life
traps: Confusing the stages of a product's life (raw material → disposal) with the four phases of an LCA study (goal & scope → interpretation). Questions may ask for either; give the one asked, and mention the other briefly.
Comparing products per item instead of per functional unit (one cloth bag is used hundreds of times; one plastic bag once or twice).
Saying LCA only considers manufacturing. It covers the whole life including use and disposal.
Writing LCI and LCIA as the same thing. Inventory is flows; impact assessment converts flows into effects.

questions.q: What is life cycle assessment (LCA)? Explain the phases of an LCA study with a diagram.
questions.a:
**LCA** is a systematic, standardised (ISO 14040/14044) method to quantify the environmental impacts of a product, process or service over its whole life cycle: raw-material extraction, manufacturing, transport, use and end-of-life ('cradle to grave').

**Diagram**: four boxes: Goal & Scope Definition → Inventory Analysis → Impact Assessment, each connected with two-way arrows to a vertical box 'Interpretation' (showing the iterative nature); outside: direct applications (product development, policy, marketing/eco-labels).

**1. Goal and scope definition**: why the study is done and for whom; the product system; the **functional unit** (quantified function, e.g. 'carrying 1000 kg of groceries'); system boundaries (which stages and processes are included); data quality, assumptions and limitations.

**2. Life cycle inventory (LCI)**: build a flow model of the system and collect data on all inputs (raw materials, energy, water) and outputs (products, emissions to air, water and soil, solid waste) for each stage, scaled to the functional unit.

**3. Life cycle impact assessment (LCIA)**: *classification*: assign inventory data to impact categories (climate change, acidification, eutrophication, ozone depletion, photochemical smog, toxicity, resource depletion); *characterisation*: convert to common units (e.g. CH$_4$ × 28 → kg CO$_2$e; SO$_2$ → kg SO$_2$e); optional normalisation and weighting.

**4. Interpretation**: identify significant issues and hotspots, carry out completeness, sensitivity and consistency checks, and draw conclusions and recommendations (e.g. redesign to cut use-phase energy).

**Applications**: eco-design, comparing alternatives, eco-labelling, green procurement, policy. **Limitations**: data-intensive, assumption-dependent, time-consuming.

questions.q: List the stages in the life cycle of a product considered in LCA.
questions.a:
1. Raw-material acquisition (extraction, mining, harvesting).
2. Material processing and manufacturing (including packaging).
3. Transportation and distribution.
4. Use, operation and maintenance.
5. End of life: reuse, recycling, recovery, incineration or landfill.

questions.q: What is a functional unit in LCA? Why is it important?
questions.a: The functional unit is a quantified description of the function the product system delivers, used as the reference to which all inputs and outputs are normalised (e.g. '1000 L of drinking water delivered', 'lighting a 10 m² room at 500 lux for 10,000 hours'). It is important because it allows a fair comparison of different products that perform the same function: e.g. one LED lamp vs several incandescent bulbs for the same hours of light.

questions.q: A product's life-cycle carbon emissions are: raw materials 2 kg, manufacture 3 kg, transport 0.5 kg, use 10 kg and end of life 0.5 kg CO₂e. Find the total and identify the hotspot.
questions.a:
Total $= 2 + 3 + 0.5 + 10 + 0.5 = 16$ kg CO$_2$e.

Use phase share $= 10/16 = 62.5\%$, so the use phase is the hotspot. Improvement should target energy efficiency during use rather than packaging or transport.

topics.why: 'Define EIA and explain the steps/process of EIA' is one of the most predictable Unit 5 questions (5-10 marks); the EIA Notification 2006 categories are a common add-on.
topics.gist:
**Environmental impact assessment (EIA)** is a process for identifying, predicting and evaluating the likely environmental, social and economic effects of a proposed project **before** it is approved, so that adverse impacts can be avoided, reduced or mitigated. It is a planning and decision-making tool, not a post-mortem.

In India EIA was made mandatory by the **EIA Notification 1994** under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986. It was replaced by the **EIA Notification 2006**, under which projects are:
- **Category A**: appraised at the central level by the MoEFCC's Expert Appraisal Committee;
- **Category B**: appraised by the State Level EIA Authority (SEIAA). **B1** projects need a full EIA; **B2** projects are exempt.

The 2006 notification lists four stages: **screening, scoping, public consultation, appraisal**.

**General EIA process** (for 'explain the steps'):
1. **Screening**: does the project need an EIA, and at what level?
2. **Scoping**: identify key issues, alternatives and terms of reference (ToR).
3. **Baseline data collection**: present state of air, water, soil, noise, ecology and the socio-economic environment.
4. **Impact prediction and evaluation**: magnitude, extent, duration and significance of impacts (positive and negative, direct and indirect, reversible and irreversible).
5. **Consideration of alternatives**: site, technology, the no-project option.
6. **Mitigation measures and an Environmental Management Plan (EMP)**.
7. **Draft EIA report**, then a **public hearing** (conducted by the SPCB), then the final EIA report.
8. **Review and decision-making**: environmental clearance granted with conditions, or rejected.
9. **Post-project monitoring** and compliance audits.

**Methods**: checklists, matrices (the **Leopold matrix**: activities × environmental components), networks and overlays (GIS). **Benefits**: prevents damage, saves costs, involves the public and supports sustainable development. **Limitations**: consultant bias, poor public participation, weak monitoring (critics of the Draft EIA Notification 2020 raised these points).
key_points: Definition and purpose of EIA (predictive, before approval).
Legal basis in India: EIA Notification 1994 → 2006 under EPA 1986.
Category A (central, EAC) vs B (state, SEIAA; B1/B2).
Four stages of the 2006 notification: screening, scoping, public consultation, appraisal.
Full EIA process steps through monitoring.
Components assessed: air, water, land, noise, biological, socio-economic.
EIA methods: checklist, matrix (Leopold), network, overlay.
Benefits and limitations.
formulas: $\text{Impact score} = \sum_{i}\sum_{j} M_{ij} \times I_{ij}$ — Leopold matrix (magnitude × importance for activity $i$ and component $j$, each typically on a 1-10 scale)
traps: Confusing EIA (project-level, before approval) with LCA (product-level, cradle to grave) or with an environmental audit (after operation).
Writing the EIA Notification year as 1986. EPA is 1986; the notifications are 1994 and 2006.
Forgetting the public hearing; it is a mandatory stage for Category A and B1 projects.
Listing steps out of order (e.g. scoping before screening).
Saying Category B is appraised by the CPCB. It is the State Level EIA Authority (SEIAA).

questions.q: What is Environmental Impact Assessment? Describe the various steps involved in the EIA process.
questions.a:
**EIA**: a systematic process of identifying, predicting, evaluating and mitigating the environmental, social and other relevant effects of a proposed development project before major decisions are taken and commitments made. In India it is mandatory under the EIA Notification 2006 (EPA 1986).

**Steps**
1. **Screening**: decide whether the project requires an EIA and at what level (Category A, B1, B2) based on type, size and location.
2. **Scoping**: identify the significant issues and impacts to study, alternatives, study area and methods; issue terms of reference (ToR).
3. **Baseline data collection**: describe existing conditions of air quality, water, soil, noise, flora and fauna, land use and socio-economic status of the area (usually one season's monitoring).
4. **Impact prediction**: predict the nature, magnitude, extent, duration and probability of impacts during construction, operation and decommissioning (models, matrices, expert judgement).
5. **Evaluation and assessment of alternatives**: compare alternative sites, technologies, designs and the no-project option; judge significance.
6. **Mitigation and Environmental Management Plan (EMP)**: measures to avoid, minimise or compensate impacts (pollution-control equipment, green belt, rehabilitation), with responsibilities and budget.
7. **Preparation of draft EIA report** with a non-technical summary.
8. **Public consultation**: public hearing conducted by the SPCB near the site and written responses from stakeholders.
9. **Final EIA report** addressing public concerns.
10. **Appraisal and decision-making**: expert committee (EAC at centre or SEAC/SEIAA at state) reviews; environmental clearance granted with conditions or rejected.
11. **Post-project monitoring and compliance**: monitoring of conditions and EMP implementation; six-monthly compliance reports.

questions.q: Write the objectives and benefits of EIA.
questions.a:
**Objectives**: (i) identify and predict environmental impacts before a project is approved; (ii) find ways to avoid or mitigate adverse impacts; (iii) select the best alternative site and technology; (iv) inform decision-makers and the public; (v) promote sustainable development.

**Benefits**: prevents costly environmental damage and later remedial work; reduces conflicts through public participation; protects natural resources and biodiversity; ensures compliance with laws; improves project design; protects the health and livelihood of affected people; provides a baseline for monitoring.

questions.q: Differentiate between screening and scoping in EIA.
questions.a: **Screening** is the first step: it decides **whether** a project needs an EIA and at what level (e.g. Category A, B1 or B2 under the 2006 Notification). **Scoping** comes next: it decides **what** the EIA must cover: the key issues and impacts, alternatives, study area, methods and the terms of reference.

questions.q: Under the EIA Notification 2006, how are Category A and Category B projects treated?
questions.a: **Category A** projects (larger scale or potentially higher impact, e.g. large mining, thermal power plants above a threshold, river valley projects) are appraised by the Expert Appraisal Committee and given clearance by the central Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. **Category B** projects (smaller scale) are appraised by the State Expert Appraisal Committee and cleared by the State Level Environment Impact Assessment Authority (SEIAA). Category B is split into **B1** (needs EIA report and public hearing) and **B2** (exempt from EIA and public hearing). A Category B project located near protected areas, inter-state boundaries or critically polluted areas is treated as Category A.

questions.q: The first step in the EIA process is:
questions.a: Screening decides whether an EIA is needed; scoping follows.

questions.q: The current EIA notification in India, under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, was issued in:
questions.a: EIA Notification 2006 (replacing the 1994 notification) is the operative notification, amended many times since.

questions.q: The Leopold matrix is used in EIA for:
options: Identifying interactions between project activities and environmental components
questions.a: It is a matrix of project activities (columns) against environmental components (rows), each cell scored for magnitude and importance.

topics.why: Every paper has at least one question on the acts (salient features, objectives, years); mixing up the years is the commonest way to lose easy marks.
topics.gist:
Indian environmental law rests on the Constitution. **Article 48A** (Directive Principle: the State shall protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife) and **Article 51A(g)** (Fundamental Duty of every citizen) were both added by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**. The courts read the right to a clean environment into **Article 21**. Parliament legislated after the **Stockholm Conference, 1972**.

Learn the five acts **in chronological order: 1972, 1974, 1980, 1981, 1986** (mnemonic **W-W-F-A-E**: Wildlife, Water, Forest, Air, Environment).

- **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972**: bans hunting of listed animals; schedules of protected species (Schedule I has the highest protection; the 2022 amendment cut six schedules to four); creates sanctuaries, national parks, and conservation and community reserves; regulates trade in wildlife products; set up the NTCA and tiger reserves (2006 amendment) and the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau.
- **Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974**: India's first pollution law. It created the **CPCB and the SPCBs**, requires **consent** to establish and operate for discharges, lets the boards set effluent standards, take samples and close polluting units. (Water Cess Act 1977.)
- **Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980**: forest land cannot be de-reserved or used for non-forest purposes without **prior approval of the Central Government** (Section 2); compensatory afforestation. Amended 1988, and in 2023 renamed the *Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam*.
- **Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981**: extended the CPCB/SPCB framework to air; declares air-pollution control areas; sets emission standards and consent for industries. **Noise was added as an air pollutant in 1987**.
- **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**: the **umbrella act**, passed after the **Bhopal gas tragedy (1984)**. Section 3 gives the Centre wide powers to protect the environment and set standards; Section 5 allows directions including closure; Section 7 bars discharges above standards. Rules made under it include the EP Rules 1986, the EIA Notification, CRZ, the Noise Rules 2000, ODS Rules 2000 and the waste-management rules.

Others: Public Liability Insurance Act 1991, **Biological Diversity Act 2002**, Forest Rights Act 2006, **National Green Tribunal Act 2010**. Penalty provisions were changed by the Jan Vishwas Act 2023 and the Water Amendment Act 2024, so check your slides before quoting penalty figures.
key_points: Constitution: Art. 48A, 51A(g) (42nd Amendment, 1976), Art. 21 (judicial interpretation).
Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972: hunting ban, schedules, protected areas, trade control.
Water Act 1974: CPCB and SPCBs, consent, standards, sampling, penalties.
Forest (Conservation) Act 1980: prior central approval for diversion of forest land.
Air Act 1981: air-pollution control areas, emission standards; noise added 1987.
Environment (Protection) Act 1986: umbrella act after Bhopal; Sections 3, 5, 7; rules under it.
Later laws: Biological Diversity Act 2002, NGT Act 2010.
traps: Swapping the years of the Water Act (1974) and Air Act (1981). Water came first; it created the CPCB.
Saying the Air Act created the CPCB. The Water Act 1974 did; the Air Act gave the same boards air functions.
Writing EPA as 1984 (the Bhopal disaster year) instead of 1986.
Saying Forest Conservation Act 1972 or Wildlife Act 1980. Wildlife is 1972; Forest is 1980.
Calling Article 51A(g) a Directive Principle. It is a Fundamental Duty; 48A is the Directive Principle.
Quoting old penalty amounts as current law without caveat. They were amended in 2023-24.

(5 marks); MCQs on years.

questions.q: Write the salient features of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
questions.a:
1. Enacted in 1986 after the Bhopal gas tragedy (1984), under Article 253, to implement the decisions of the Stockholm Conference (1972); in force from 19 November 1986. Called an **umbrella act** because it fills the gaps of earlier laws.
2. Defines environment (water, air, land and their inter-relationship with humans, other living beings and property), environmental pollutant and hazardous substance.
3. **Section 3**: the Central Government can take all measures to protect and improve the environment: lay down standards for environmental quality and emissions/discharges, restrict industries in certain areas, set procedures for handling hazardous substances, inspect, and constitute authorities.
4. **Section 5**: power to issue directions, including closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry and stopping electricity or water supply.
5. **Section 7**: no person shall discharge pollutants in excess of prescribed standards; **Section 8**: handling of hazardous substances only per procedure.
6. Powers of entry, inspection, sampling, and environmental laboratories and analysts.
7. Penalties for contravention (originally up to 5 years' imprisonment and/or fine up to ₹1 lakh, with more for continuing offences; since revised by the Jan Vishwas Act 2023).
8. Citizen's right to complain after 60 days' notice.
9. Many rules framed under it: EP Rules 1986, EIA Notification (1994/2006), CRZ Notification, Hazardous/Bio-medical/Solid/Plastic/E-waste Rules, Noise Rules 2000, ODS Rules 2000.

questions.q: Write the main provisions of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974.
questions.a:
1. First major environmental law of India; aims to prevent and control water pollution and maintain or restore the wholesomeness of water.
2. Constitutes the **Central Pollution Control Board** and **State Pollution Control Boards**.
3. Functions of the boards: plan programmes, advise governments, lay down effluent and water-quality standards, collect and publish data, inspect treatment plants, train personnel.
4. **Consent** of the SPCB is required to establish or operate any industry or process that discharges sewage or trade effluent.
5. Boards can take samples of effluents, enter and inspect premises, and direct closure or stoppage of water and power supply to defaulting units.
6. Prohibits discharge of poisonous or polluting matter into streams and wells beyond standards.
7. Penalties for violations (amended in 1988 and again in 2024).
8. Supplemented by the Water Cess Act 1977 for funding the boards.

questions.q: Write short notes on (a) Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 and (b) Forest (Conservation) Act 1980.
questions.a:
**(a) Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972**: provides for protection of wild animals, birds and plants. Prohibits hunting of scheduled animals; lists species in schedules with different protection levels (Schedule I highest; rationalised to four schedules in 2022); provides for sanctuaries, national parks, and (from 2002) conservation and community reserves; regulates trade in wildlife and their products; constitutes the National Board for Wildlife; 2006 amendment created the National Tiger Conservation Authority and Wildlife Crime Control Bureau; penalties for offences. Example in Bhopal: Van Vihar National Park.

**(b) Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980**: enacted to check rapid deforestation. Under Section 2, no state government can, without **prior approval of the Central Government**, de-reserve a reserved forest, use forest land for any non-forest purpose, lease it to private bodies, or clear naturally grown trees for reafforestation. Provides an advisory committee; compensatory afforestation is a condition of approval (CAMPA). Amended in 1988 and, in 2023, renamed the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam.

questions.q: List the major environmental laws of India in chronological order with their years.
questions.a:
1. Wildlife (Protection) Act, **1972**
2. Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, **1974** (Water Cess Act 1977)
3. Forest (Conservation) Act, **1980**
4. Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, **1981** (noise added 1987)
5. Environment (Protection) Act, **1986**
6. Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991
7. Biological Diversity Act, 2002
8. National Green Tribunal Act, 2010

Constitutional basis: Articles 48A and 51A(g), added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).

questions.a: The CPCB and SPCBs were created by the Water Act 1974; the Air Act 1981 gave them air-pollution functions.

questions.q: The Environment (Protection) Act was enacted in the year:
questions.a: 1986, in the aftermath of the 1984 Bhopal gas tragedy.

questions.a: Article 51A(g) is the Fundamental Duty; Article 48A is the Directive Principle for the State; both were added in 1976.

topics.why: 'State and explain the twelve principles of green chemistry' is a standard 10-mark question; atom economy gives a quick numerical.
topics.gist:
**Green chemistry** (sustainable chemistry) is the design of chemical products and processes that **reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances** (Paul Anastas and John Warner, 1998). It prevents pollution at the molecular level instead of treating it at the end of the pipe.

**The twelve principles** (learn them in order):
1. **Prevention**: it is better to prevent waste than to treat or clean it up.
2. **Atom economy**: incorporate as many reactant atoms as possible into the final product.
3. **Less hazardous chemical syntheses**: use and generate substances of little or no toxicity.
4. **Designing safer chemicals**: products that do their job with minimal toxicity.
5. **Safer solvents and auxiliaries**: avoid them or use benign ones (water, supercritical CO$_2$, ionic liquids, solvent-free reactions).
6. **Design for energy efficiency**: run reactions at ambient temperature and pressure (microwave or ultrasound help).
7. **Use of renewable feedstocks**: biomass instead of petroleum.
8. **Reduce derivatives**: avoid unnecessary protecting groups and temporary modifications.
9. **Catalysis**: catalytic (selective) reagents are better than stoichiometric ones.
10. **Design for degradation**: products break down into harmless substances after use.
11. **Real-time analysis for pollution prevention**: in-process monitoring before hazardous substances form.
12. **Inherently safer chemistry for accident prevention**: choose substances and forms that minimise the risk of explosions, fires and releases (Bhopal is the lesson).

**Metrics**: atom economy, and the **E-factor** (kg of waste per kg of product). E-factors run from about 0.1 for oil refining to 25-100 or more for pharmaceuticals.

**Examples**: the BHC synthesis of **ibuprofen** (3 catalytic steps, ~77% atom economy, against ~40% for the 6-step Boots route), supercritical CO$_2$ for dry-cleaning and decaffeination, H$_2$O$_2$ as a clean oxidant, biodegradable polylactic acid from corn starch, enzymatic processes, and adipic acid from glucose instead of benzene.
key_points: Definition; Anastas and Warner (1998).
All 12 principles in order with a one-line explanation and an example each.
Atom economy formula and examples (addition 100%, substitution/elimination lower).
E-factor and typical ranges by industry.
Green solvents: water, supercritical CO₂, ionic liquids, solvent-free.
Classic examples: ibuprofen BHC process, PLA, H₂O₂ oxidation, sc-CO₂ dry-cleaning.
Why it matters: pollution prevention at source, safety, cost.
formulas: $\text{Atom economy (\%)} = \dfrac{\text{molar mass of desired product}}{\sum \text{molar masses of all reactants}} \times 100$
$E\text{-factor} = \dfrac{\text{total mass of waste (kg)}}{\text{mass of product (kg)}}$
$\text{Percentage yield} = \dfrac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$ — not the same as atom economy
traps: Confusing atom economy with percentage yield. A reaction can have 100% yield and poor atom economy.
Listing fewer than 12 principles, or merging 'prevention' and 'atom economy'.
Calling catalysis 'use of stoichiometric reagents'. The principle prefers CATALYTIC over stoichiometric reagents.
Saying green chemistry means treating waste better. It is about not producing it (prevention at source).
Putting the ten commandments of sustainability in place of the twelve principles of green chemistry, or the reverse.

questions.q: What is green chemistry? State and explain the twelve principles of green chemistry.
questions.a:
**Green chemistry** is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances across the life cycle (Anastas and Warner, 1998).

1. **Prevention**: preventing waste is better than treating or cleaning it after it is formed.
2. **Atom economy**: synthetic methods should maximise incorporation of all materials used into the final product (addition reactions such as Diels-Alder have 100% atom economy).
3. **Less hazardous chemical syntheses**: methods should use and generate substances with little or no toxicity to humans and the environment (e.g. avoid phosgene, use dimethyl carbonate).
4. **Designing safer chemicals**: products should perform their function with minimal toxicity (e.g. less toxic pesticides).
5. **Safer solvents and auxiliaries**: avoid auxiliary substances where possible; otherwise use innocuous ones like water, supercritical CO$_2$, ionic liquids, or solvent-free conditions.
6. **Design for energy efficiency**: conduct reactions at ambient temperature and pressure; use microwave or ultrasound activation.
7. **Use of renewable feedstocks**: use biomass (starch, cellulose, vegetable oils) rather than depleting petroleum.
8. **Reduce derivatives**: avoid unnecessary blocking/protecting groups and temporary modifications, which need extra reagents and create waste.
9. **Catalysis**: catalytic reagents (as selective as possible, e.g. enzymes, zeolites) are superior to stoichiometric reagents.
10. **Design for degradation**: products should break down into harmless products after use and not persist (e.g. biodegradable polymers like PLA instead of persistent plastics).
11. **Real-time analysis for pollution prevention**: in-process monitoring and control before hazardous substances form.
12. **Inherently safer chemistry for accident prevention**: choose substances and their physical forms to minimise the potential for accidents, explosions, fires and releases (e.g. avoid storing large quantities of MIC, as at Bhopal).

**Example**: BHC process for ibuprofen: 3 catalytic steps, ~77% atom economy (≈99% with acetic acid by-product recovered), compared with the 6-step Boots process (~40%).

questions.q: Calculate the atom economy for the preparation of ethanol from bromoethane: $\mathrm{C_2H_5Br + NaOH \rightarrow C_2H_5OH + NaBr}$ (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23, Br = 80).
questions.a:
Molar masses: C$_2$H$_5$Br = 24 + 5 + 80 = 109; NaOH = 40; C$_2$H$_5$OH = 46.

$\text{Atom economy} = \dfrac{46}{109 + 40} \times 100 = \dfrac{46}{149} \times 100 \approx 30.9\%$

Only about 31% of reactant mass ends in the product; the rest becomes NaBr waste, so substitution reactions have poor atom economy compared with addition reactions (100%).

questions.q: Differentiate between atom economy and percentage yield.
questions.a: **Percentage yield** compares the actual amount of product obtained with the theoretical maximum: (actual/theoretical) × 100. It measures how well a reaction was carried out. **Atom economy** compares the mass of the desired product with the total mass of all reactants: (M product / Σ M reactants) × 100. It measures how much of the reactants can, in principle, end up in the product, i.e. inherent waste. A reaction can have 100% yield but low atom economy (e.g. Wittig reaction producing Ph$_3$PO waste).

questions.q: Give three examples of green solvents and one advantage of each.
questions.a:
1. **Water**: non-toxic, non-flammable, cheap, abundant.
2. **Supercritical CO$_2$**: non-toxic, non-flammable, easily removed by depressurising, leaves no residue; used for decaffeination and dry-cleaning.
3. **Ionic liquids**: negligible vapour pressure (no VOC emission), recyclable, tunable.
(Also: solvent-free reactions, bio-based solvents like ethyl lactate.)

questions.q: Which type of reaction has 100% atom economy?
questions.a: In an addition reaction all reactant atoms end up in the single product, so atom economy is 100%.

questions.q: The principle 'catalytic reagents are superior to stoichiometric reagents' is which principle of green chemistry?
questions.a: Principle 9 is catalysis. 1 is prevention, 5 safer solvents, 12 accident prevention.

questions.q: A process produces 1 kg of a drug and generates 50 kg of waste. What is its E-factor and what does it indicate?
questions.a: $E = \dfrac{50}{1} = 50$. This is typical of fine-chemical and pharmaceutical processes (E ~ 5-100) and indicates a lot of waste per kg product, mostly solvents; green chemistry aims to reduce it towards zero.

topics.why: Defining sustainable development (Brundtland) is a sure 2-mark question, and the 'ten commandments' is a list the teacher will expect reproduced as a 5-10 mark answer. The exact list should be checked against the class slides.
topics.gist:
**Sustainable development** is 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs' (**Brundtland Report, *Our Common Future*, 1987**). It rests on three pillars, **environmental, economic and social** (the triple bottom line: people, planet, profit), and on equity both **between** and **within** generations.

**Milestones**: Stockholm Conference 1972 (UNEP); Brundtland 1987; Rio Earth Summit 1992 (**Agenda 21**, conventions on climate change and biodiversity); Johannesburg 2002; Rio+20 2012; the **17 Sustainable Development Goals** (2015, target 2030); the Paris Agreement 2015.

The pressure on the environment is captured by **IPAT**: Impact = Population × Affluence × Technology. Sustainability means living within the Earth's **carrying capacity**, using renewables no faster than they regenerate and producing waste no faster than nature can absorb it.

**The 'ten commandments' of sustainability**: Indian EVS courses present a list of ten rules for sustainable living. The wording varies by teacher, so match your slides. The standard content is:
1. Conserve natural resources and use them efficiently, within carrying capacity.
2. Reduce, reuse and recycle; minimise waste.
3. Shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy and save energy.
4. Prevent pollution at source; the polluter pays.
5. Protect biodiversity, forests and ecosystems.
6. Stabilise population growth.
7. Practise sustainable agriculture and water use.
8. Ensure equity between and within generations (alleviate poverty, fair sharing).
9. Use appropriate, clean technology and follow the precautionary principle.
10. Promote environmental education, public participation and good governance, and integrate environment into economic decisions.

At the individual level this means consuming less, choosing durable and local products, and voting and acting for the environment.

Three pillars / triple bottom line; inter- and intra-generational equity.
Milestones: Stockholm 1972, Brundtland 1987, Rio 1992 (Agenda 21), SDGs 2015 (17 goals, 2030).
IPAT equation; carrying capacity; strong vs weak sustainability.
The ten commandments (as in class slides) with one line each.
Individual and institutional actions for sustainability.

questions.q: Define sustainable development and explain its three pillars.
questions.a:
**Definition** (Brundtland Commission, *Our Common Future*, 1987): 'Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.'

**Three pillars**
1. **Environmental sustainability**: use renewable resources within their regeneration rate, non-renewables prudently and with substitution, keep pollution within the assimilative capacity, conserve biodiversity and ecosystems.
2. **Economic sustainability**: long-term economic growth and livelihoods, resource efficiency, accounting for environmental costs (green GDP), polluter-pays.
3. **Social sustainability**: equity, poverty reduction, health, education, gender equality, participation and cultural preservation; equity between and within generations.

Development is sustainable only where all three overlap (triple bottom line: people, planet, profit).

questions.q: Explain the ten commandments of sustainability.
questions.a:
1. **Conserve resources**: use natural resources efficiently and within the carrying capacity of the Earth; harvest renewables no faster than they regenerate.
2. **Reduce, reuse, recycle**: minimise waste generation; close material loops (circular economy).
3. **Clean energy**: save energy and shift from fossil fuels to renewable sources (solar, wind, biomass, hydro).
4. **Prevent pollution at source**: cleaner production; polluter-pays principle.
5. **Protect biodiversity**: conserve forests, wildlife, wetlands and ecosystems that provide life-support services.
6. **Stabilise population**: family planning, education and health, so that numbers stay within carrying capacity.
7. **Sustainable agriculture and water use**: organic/IPM practices, soil conservation, efficient irrigation, rainwater harvesting.
8. **Equity**: fair sharing of resources and benefits within the present generation (poverty alleviation) and with future generations.
9. **Appropriate technology and precaution**: use clean, local, low-impact technologies; where damage is uncertain but serious, act to prevent it (precautionary principle).
10. **Awareness, participation and governance**: environmental education, people's participation and integration of environmental concerns in economic planning and law.

(Note: the wording of the ten commandments varies between texts; reproduce the list given in class if it differs.)

questions.q: Explain the IPAT equation with an example.
questions.a: $I = P \times A \times T$: environmental **I**mpact equals **P**opulation × **A**ffluence (consumption per person) × **T**echnology (impact per unit of consumption). Example: if a city's population doubles and per-capita car use stays the same, emissions double; but if vehicles become twice as efficient (T halves), impact stays the same. It shows that sustainability needs action on all three factors: population, consumption and cleaner technology.

questions.q: Write a short note on the Sustainable Development Goals.
questions.a: The SDGs were adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2015 as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development: **17 goals** with 169 targets, succeeding the 8 Millennium Development Goals. They include no poverty, zero hunger, good health, quality education, gender equality, clean water and sanitation (6), affordable and clean energy (7), decent work, industry and innovation, reduced inequality, sustainable cities, responsible consumption and production (12), climate action (13), life below water (14), life on land (15), peace and justice, and partnerships. They are universal, integrated and apply to all countries; India's NITI Aayog tracks progress through the SDG India Index.

questions.q: The definition of sustainable development as 'meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs' was given in:
questions.a: The Brundtland Commission report 'Our Common Future' (1987).

questions.q: How many Sustainable Development Goals were adopted by the UN in 2015?
questions.a: 17 SDGs with 169 targets, to be achieved by 2030. The 8 goals were the earlier MDGs.
